title: Physical Models of Living Systems
text:
Scope
These are lecture notes for Physical Models of Living Systems (Master in Physics of Data, University of Padova; Profs. Samir Suweis and Amos Maritan). The course uses the vocabulary of statistical physics to model biological systems at scales from a single microbial population to a whole brain and the inside of a cell: master equations, mean-field limits, phase transitions, random matrices, maximum entropy and criticality.
The notes follow the three modules of the course:

Part I: Ecology. Deterministic and stochastic population dynamics; neutral theory and the upscaling of biodiversity; spatial and temporal macroecological patterns and metapopulations; predator–prey dynamics and stochastic amplification; random matrices and the complexity–stability paradox; mutualistic networks, consumer–resource models and metabolic scaling.
Part II: Neuroscience. The brain and how it is measured; single-neuron models and spike statistics; firing-rate networks and Wilson–Cowan dynamics; Hebbian plasticity and Hopfield networks; Boltzmann machines; whole-brain models and brain criticality.
Part III: Physics of the cell. The cell and gene regulation; thermodynamics at the micro-scale and molecular motors; stochastic gene expression and genetic circuits; inference of interaction networks by maximum entropy; proteins as compact polymers.

How the notes are organised
Each chapter follows the official course notes and the lecture slides of the 2025–26 edition. The books listed below supply depth and examples. Definitions, theorems, worked examples and remarks are set in callouts. Every chapter ends with exercises: the course homework (marked HW), the class exercises (notebooks on Oja’s rule, Hopfield networks and datasets), and further problems, all with worked solutions. Numerical results quoted in solutions were checked by simulation or direct computation.

Notation

\(n\), \(N(t)\): population sizes; \(P_n(t)\) or \(P(x, t)\): probability of a state; \(x = n/N\) a density.
\(W^\pm(n)\), \(T(n \to n')\): transition rates; \(A(x)\), \(B(x)\): drift and diffusion in Fokker–Planck equations.
\(r_i\), \(K_i\), \(M_{ij}\): growth rates, carrying capacities and interactions in Lotka–Volterra models; \(J\): the Jacobian (community matrix).
\(\phi\), \(r\): firing rates; \(W_{ij}\): synaptic weights; \(s_i \in \{\pm1\}\) or \(\{0, 1\}\): binary neural states; \(E\), \(H\): energy functions; \(\beta = 1/T\).
\(m\), \(p\): mRNA and protein numbers in gene-expression models.

title: 1  Introduction: living systems as complex systems
text:
1.1 Three systems, one framework
Biology offers systems in which many simple units interact: individuals in an ecosystem, neurons in a brain, genes and proteins in a cell. The behaviour of the whole is not written in any single unit, yet it is often surprisingly simple and reproducible across systems that share little microscopic detail. This course uses the tools of statistical physics to explain such regularities: master equations, mean-field limits, phase transitions, random matrices and criticality. This chapter sets out the programme, the empirical patterns we want to explain, and the modelling philosophy behind them.
The course has three modules, each studied with the same sequence of questions:
For each we ask how the units evolve, first deterministically (ordinary differential equations for mean quantities) and then stochastically (master equations, Fokker–Planck and Langevin equations), and which collective, emergent properties appear when many units interact.
Emergent behaviour would be of little use if it were as intricate as the microscopic details. The reason a physicist can contribute is that, very often, it is not. Interacting units produce simple patterns (power laws, universal distributions, sharp transitions) that recur across systems with completely different microscopic rules. That recurrence suggests common principles that a minimal model can capture. Throughout the course we look for the null model: the simplest mechanism that reproduces an observed pattern. Departures from it then tell us which biological detail actually matters.

text:
Ecological systems
Neural networks
Genetic circuits




one unit
a single species
a single neuron
a single gene


two units
predator and prey
excitatory and inhibitory populations
a regulator and its target


many units
communities, food webs
recurrent networks, the whole brain
regulatory networks





A complex system is made of many units whose interactions, rather than whose individual properties, determine the macroscopic behaviour. A property is emergent if it belongs to the system as a whole and cannot be deduced from any single component taken in isolation.








The 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared by G. Parisi “for the discovery of the interplay of disorder and fluctuations in physical systems from atomic to planetary scales”, recognised precisely this programme. Several tools of this course (random matrices, replica calculations, spin-glass-like energy landscapes) come from that tradition.

title: 1  Introduction: living systems as complex systems
text:
1.2 Two motivating examples

The catch record of Atlantic cod over the twentieth century oscillates with the reproductive cycle and shows a huge peak in the 1960s, driven by industrial fishing. After a smaller secondary maximum, the fishery collapsed abruptly in the early 1990s and never recovered, even after fishing stopped. The collapse is not a smooth decline proportional to the fishing effort. It is a critical transition, a jump between two qualitatively different states of the ecosystem.


Deaths from malaria are distributed very unevenly across the globe. Their statistics are strongly heterogeneous, with a few areas carrying most of the burden. Homogeneous fluctuations are well described by Gaussian statistics with a typical scale. Heterogeneous ones are typically described by power-law (scale-free) distributions, in which no single scale dominates. Which mechanism produces one shape or the other is a recurring theme of the course.

title: 1  Introduction: living systems as complex systems
text:
1.3 Emergent ecological patterns
Ecology offers the cleanest examples of universal patterns. They are measured by counting individuals of each species in plots of increasing size.

The SAR \(S(A)\) is the mean number of species found in an area \(A\). Over a wide range of intermediate scales it is well fitted by a power law \[S(A) = c\,A^{z}, \qquad z \approx 0.2\text{–}0.3,\] for plants, birds, amphibians and mammals, on every continent: the curves differ in the prefactor \(c\) but share the shape.


The EAR \(E(A)\) is the number of species found only inside an area \(A\) (endemic to it). It rises slowly at small areas and steeply near the size of the whole region. Since destroying an area \(A\) wipes out the species endemic to it, the EAR is the right tool to estimate extinctions from habitat loss (Chapter 4).


The RSA, or species abundance distribution (SAD), \(P(n)\), is the fraction of species represented by \(n\) individuals. Empirical RSAs have a characteristic shape: many rare species and few very abundant ones. They are classically fitted by Fisher’s log-series or Preston’s log-normal, and neutral theory predicts them from first principles (Chapter 3).

A second celebrated regularity concerns metabolism.

Across organisms whose masses span more than twenty orders of magnitude, from bacteria to whales, the metabolic rate \(B\) scales with body mass \(M\) as \[B = B_0\,M^{a}, \qquad a \simeq 3/4 .\] Many other traits follow from it as power laws of \(M\): lifespan \(\propto M^{1/4}\), heartbeat frequency \(\propto M^{-1/4}\), and population density \(\propto M^{-3/4}\).

Since a \(3/4\) exponent differs from the “surface-to-volume” value \(2/3\), its explanation (West, Brown and Enquist’s optimal transport networks, or Banavar, Maritan and Rinaldo’s argument on supply networks) is a classic problem in biological physics. We return to metabolic scaling and its consequences for coexistence in Chapter 7.

section: 1.4 A short history of population dynamics
text:
1.4 A short history of population dynamics
Population modelling is as old as quantitative science:

Fibonacci (1202) counted rabbits, producing the first growth law with a characteristic ratio.
Euler (1748) wrote exponential growth, \(\dot N = rN\).
Malthus (1798) argued that unchecked populations grow geometrically while resources grow at most arithmetically.
Verhulst (1838) added self-limitation, \(\dot N = rN(1 - N/K)\), the logistic equation, which predicts a steady state.

Chapter 2 shows how these laws can be derived, rather than postulated, from symmetry and from resource dynamics.

section: 1.5 Critical transitions and alternative stable states
text:
1.5 Critical transitions and alternative stable states
The cod collapse illustrates a mechanism we will meet repeatedly: a system can have two stable states for the same environmental conditions, and slow changes in a parameter can make one of them disappear.

A resource (vegetation, fish stock) grows logistically and is consumed by a predator whose consumption saturates: \[\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\Bigl(1 - \frac{N}{K}\Bigr) - c\,\frac{N^2}{N_0^2 + N^2}.\] For small consumption pressure \(c\) there is a single, high-abundance equilibrium. Over an intermediate range of \(c\) a second, low-abundance stable equilibrium appears, separated from the first by an unstable one. Increasing \(c\) beyond a threshold \(c_2\) makes the high branch collide with the unstable branch and vanish (a saddle-node, or fold, bifurcation): the population drops to the low branch. To recover the high state one must reduce \(c\) well below \(c_2\), down to the other fold \(c_1 < c_2\) (hysteresis).


Figure: equilibrium abundance against consumption pressure. Solid: stable branches; dashed: unstable branch. Crossing a fold produces a jump; recovery requires going back to the other fold.
Near a fold the stabilising eigenvalue tends to zero, so perturbations decay more and more slowly. This critical slowing down gives measurable early-warning signals of an approaching collapse: rising variance and rising autocorrelation of fluctuations. Chapter 5 adds the stochastic side of the story, where demographic noise near a weakly stable equilibrium is amplified into large, coherent oscillations.

1.6 How to read these notes

Part I (ecology) builds the toolbox: master equations and their continuum limits (Chapter 2), neutral theory and scaling (Chapters 3–4), interacting species and random matrices (Chapters 5–7).
Part II (neuroscience) reuses it for neurons and networks: single-neuron models, firing-rate networks, learning and memory, and brain criticality (Chapters 8–13).
Part III (physics of the cell) applies it inside the cell: gene expression, molecular machines, regulatory circuits, inference of interaction networks and proteins (Chapters 14–18).

Each chapter ends with exercises. They include the course homework (marked HW), whose solutions are worked out in full.

title: 1  Introduction: living systems as complex systems
text:
1.7 Exercises

(Scaling from a SAR) Suppose \(S(A) = cA^z\) with \(z = 0.25\). (a) By what factor does the number of species grow when the area grows tenfold? (b) If a habitat loses half its area, what fraction of species does the SAR predict to be lost? (c) Why is (b) only a rough estimate of extinctions?


Solution. 

\(10^{0.25} = 1.78\): a tenfold area holds about \(78\%\) more species. (b) \(S(A/2)/S(A) = 2^{-0.25} = 0.84\), so about \(16\%\) of species are “lost”. (c) The SAR counts species present in a sample of area \(A/2\); species that also live in the destroyed half survive there. The species that disappear are those endemic to the destroyed part, which the EAR measures (Chapter 4). Using the SAR overestimates extinctions caused by habitat loss.



(Kleiber scaling) With \(B \propto M^{3/4}\), compare the metabolic rate per unit mass of a \(3\) g shrew and a \(3000\) kg elephant. How does the energy needed per kilogram compare?


Solution. \(B/M \propto M^{-1/4}\). The mass ratio is \(10^6\), so the shrew needs \((10^6)^{1/4} \approx 32\) times more energy per kilogram than the elephant. Small animals live “faster”: with lifespan \(\propto M^{1/4}\), the total energy spent per kilogram over a lifetime, \(\propto M^{-1/4}M^{1/4}\), is roughly independent of size.


(Fisher’s log-series) Suppose the number of species with \(n\) individuals is \(\phi_n = \theta\,x^n/n\), with \(0 < x < 1\). Compute the number of species \(S\) and individuals \(J\). Show that for \(J \gg \theta\), \(S \simeq \theta\ln(1 + J/\theta)\).


Solution. \(S = \sum_{n\geq1}\theta x^n/n = -\theta\ln(1 - x)\) and \(J = \sum_{n\geq1}n\phi_n = \theta\sum_{n\geq1}x^n = \theta\,\frac{x}{1-x}\). From the second, \(1 - x = \theta/(J + \theta)\), so \(S = \theta\ln\bigl(1 + J/\theta\bigr)\), exactly. Species richness grows only logarithmically with the number of sampled individuals. \(\theta\), the fundamental biodiversity number, sets the rate. Neutral theory gives it a meaning (Chapter 3).


(Fold bifurcation) For \(\dot x = r + x^2\), find the equilibria and their stability as a function of \(r\). Show that the relaxation time near the stable equilibrium diverges as \(r \to 0^-\), and give the exponent.


Solution. For \(r < 0\) the equilibria are \(x_\pm = \pm\sqrt{-r}\). The derivative of the right-hand side is \(2x\), so \(x_- = -\sqrt{-r}\) is stable (eigenvalue \(-2\sqrt{-r}\)) and \(x_+\) unstable. For \(r > 0\) there are none. Linearising, perturbations decay as \(e^{-2\sqrt{-r}\,t}\), with relaxation time \(\tau = 1/(2\sqrt{|r|})\), which diverges with exponent \(1/2\). This is critical slowing down. Any noise-driven fluctuations then have a variance \(\propto \tau\) that grows as the fold approaches: an early-warning signal.


(Hysteresis in the grazing model) In May’s grazing model set \(r = N_0 = 1\), so \(\dot N = N(1 - N/K) - cN^2/(1 + N^2)\). (a) Show that the positive equilibria satisfy \(c = c(N) \equiv (1 - N/K)(1 + N^2)/N\). (b) For \(K = 1\) and \(K = 10\), find the range of \(c\) with three positive equilibria.


Solution. 

Dividing \(\dot N = 0\) by \(N > 0\) gives \(1 - N/K = cN/(1 + N^2)\). Each horizontal line $c = $ const crosses the curve \(c(N)\) once per equilibrium. (b) For \(K = 1\), \(c(N)\) is monotonically decreasing on \((0, 1)\): one equilibrium for every \(c\), and no bistability. For \(K = 10\), \(c(N)\) has a local minimum \(c_1 \approx 1.79\) (at \(N \approx 1.14\)) and a local maximum \(c_2 \approx 2.60\) (at \(N \approx 4.78\)). For \(c_1 < c < c_2\) there are three positive equilibria: the lowest and highest are stable, the middle one unstable. Alternative stable states need a separation of scales between the carrying capacity \(K\) and the saturation scale \(N_0\) of consumption.

title: 2  Dynamics of a single species
text:
2.1 Basic microbiology
We start from the simplest living system that can be modelled quantitatively: one population of bacteria. The chapter has two halves. The deterministic half derives exponential and logistic growth from a symmetry argument and from an explicit model of resource consumption. The stochastic half replaces the population by a random variable, writes its master equation, and develops the tools used throughout the course: stationary solutions and detailed balance, the Gillespie algorithm, the Fokker–Planck and Langevin limits, and first-passage problems such as the timing of cell division.
A bacterium such as Escherichia coli is a rod roughly \(2\)–\(4\,\mu\)m long and \(0.8\,\mu\)m wide. It is enclosed by an inner membrane, a cell wall and (in Gram-negative species) an outer membrane, and it contains a “soup” of DNA, RNA, proteins and small molecules. Nutrients from the surrounding medium cross the membranes and are converted into biomass by metabolism. When the cell reaches a critical size it divides into two daughters (binary fission). In rich medium at \(37\,^\circ\)C, E. coli divides every \(\tau \approx 20\) minutes.
DNA is a sequence of nucleotides (bases A, C, G, T) organised into genes. To a first approximation each gene can be treated as a binary variable, on when it is transcribed and its protein produced, off otherwise. This picture becomes quantitative in Part III.

title: 2  Dynamics of a single species
text:
2.2 Deterministic growth laws

2.2.1 Growth laws from scale invariance
Let \(N(t)\) be the number of individuals living in an area (or volume) \(A\), and suppose the growth rate depends only on these two quantities, \(\dot N = F(N, A)\). If we consider \(\lambda\) identical, independent copies of the system, the total population must obey the same law: \[F(\lambda N, \lambda A) = \lambda F(N, A).\] \(F\) is homogeneous of degree one. Choosing \(\lambda = 1/A\) gives \(F(N, A) = A\,F(N/A, 1) \equiv A f(\rho)\), so the density \(\rho = N/A\) obeys an autonomous equation \[\dot\rho = f(\rho).\] Expanding \(f\) for small densities, \[f(\rho) = f_0 + f_1\rho + \tfrac12 f_2\rho^2 + \dots,\] each coefficient has a meaning:

\(f_0 > 0\) describes immigration into an open system; \(f_0 = 0\) for a closed population, which must stay extinct once extinct.
\(f_1 = r\) is the per-capita growth rate at low density. If \(f_1 > 0\) the empty state is unstable and the population grows exponentially.
\(f_2 < 0\) describes self-limitation (crowding, competition for resources).

Truncating at second order with \(f_0 = 0\), \(f_1 = r > 0\), \(f_2 = -2r/K\) gives the logistic law. It is the generic behaviour of a closed population near extinction and near saturation, not an ad hoc guess.

Exponential growth: \(\dot N = \mu N\), so \(N(t) = N_0e^{\mu t} = N_0\,2^{t/T}\), with doubling time \(T = \ln 2/\mu\). For E. coli in optimal conditions \(\mu \simeq 2.1\,\mathrm h^{-1}\), so \(T \simeq 20\) min.
Logistic growth (Verhulst, 1838): with carrying capacity \(K\), \[\dot N = \mu N\Bigl(1 - \frac{N}{K}\Bigr), \qquad N(t) = \frac{N_0e^{\mu t}}{1 + \frac{N_0}{K}\bigl(e^{\mu t} - 1\bigr)} .\]

The solution follows by separation of variables, \(\int \frac{dN}{N(1 - N/K)} = \mu t\), and partial fractions. A bacterial batch culture fits it well: an exponential phase while \(N \ll K\), a saturation (stationary) phase as \(N \to K\). A real culture also has an initial lag phase, during which cells adapt to the new medium.

Figure: logistic growth from below and from above the carrying capacity (bold), and the exponential law with the same initial condition (thin).


2.2.2 Linear stability
An equilibrium \(N^*\) of \(\dot N = F(N)\) is stable if small perturbations decay. Writing \(N = N^* + \delta\) and expanding, \(\dot\delta = F'(N^*)\delta\), so \(N^*\) is stable if \(F'(N^*) < 0\), with relaxation time \(1/|F'(N^*)|\). For the logistic law \(F'(N) = \mu(1 - 2N/K)\): \(N^* = 0\) has \(F'(0) = \mu > 0\) (unstable) and \(N^* = K\) has \(F'(K) = -\mu\) (stable, relaxation time \(1/\mu\)).
For systems of equations \(\dot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf F(\mathbf x)\), the role of \(F'\) is played by the Jacobian \(J_{ij} = \partial F_i/\partial x_j\) at the equilibrium. The equilibrium is stable iff all its eigenvalues have negative real part. This criterion will be the starting point of the random-matrix analysis of Chapter 6.

title: 2  Dynamics of a single species
text:
2.3 Consumer–resource models
The carrying capacity hides the resource. To make it explicit, let \(R(t)\) be the amount of resource, \(g(R)\) the uptake rate per cell, \(\mu(R)\) the resource’s own supply or growth, \(\gamma\) the yield (cells produced per unit of resource), \(c\) an uptake efficiency (set to \(1\) below) and \(d\) the death rate: \[\dot N = \bigl(\gamma c\,g(R) - d\bigr)N, \qquad \dot R = \mu(R) - c\,g(R)\,N .\] Common uptake functions are linear, \(g(R) = qR\) (mass action), and saturating, the Monod law \[g(R) = \frac{q_M R}{K_M + R},\] which states that a cell cannot process resource faster than \(q_M\). \(K_M\) is the concentration at which uptake is half-maximal.

If the resource relaxes much faster than the population, then on the population’s time scale \(R\) is always at its instantaneous equilibrium, found by setting \(\dot R = 0\) at fixed \(N\). Substituting it into \(\dot N\) gives a closed equation for \(N\) alone. This is adiabatic elimination of a fast variable, and it is used throughout physics and biochemistry (Michaelis–Menten kinetics is the same idea).

Biotic resource (MacArthur). If the resource is itself a living population with logistic growth, \(\mu(R) = r^*R(1 - R/k_c)\), and uptake is linear, then \[\dot N = N(\gamma cR - d), \qquad \dot R = R\Bigl[r^*\Bigl(1 - \frac{R}{k_c}\Bigr) - cN\Bigr].\] The QSA with \(R \neq 0\) gives \(R^* = k_c\bigl(1 - cN/r^*\bigr)\), and substituting, \[\dot N = N\bigl(\tilde k - \tilde a N\bigr), \qquad \tilde k = \gamma ck_c - d, \quad \tilde a = \frac{\gamma c^2k_c}{r^*},\] a logistic law with growth rate \(\mu = \tilde k\) and carrying capacity \(K = \tilde k/\tilde a\). The carrying capacity is now derived from the resource’s parameters. The population survives only if \(\gamma ck_c > d\): the resource must be able to sustain more births than deaths.
Abiotic resource. If the resource is supplied at a constant rate, \(\mu(R) = C\) (a chemostat), the QSA gives \(g(R)N = C\) and then \[\dot N = \gamma C - dN, \qquad N^* = \frac{\gamma C}{d},\] whatever the uptake function: the population relaxes linearly to \(N^*\) with time constant \(1/d\), not logistically. The uptake function only fixes the resource level at equilibrium, through \(\gamma g(R^*) = d\): \[R^*_{\text{linear}} = \frac{d}{\gamma q}, \qquad R^*_{\text{Monod}} = \frac{K_Md}{\gamma q_M - d}.\] With Monod uptake a population can persist only if \(\gamma q_M > d\), i.e. if its maximal growth beats death. The QSA also requires \(C/N < q_M\): a small population cannot consume all the supplied resource, which then accumulates.

title: 2  Dynamics of a single species
text:
2.4 Stochastic population dynamics
Populations are made of discrete individuals, and births and deaths are random events. Deterministic equations describe the mean behaviour of large populations. Near extinction, or in small populations, demographic noise dominates.






NoteRates and probabilities



A process occurring at rate \(r\) produces, in a time \(t\), a Poisson number of independent events: \(\Pr[k \text{ events}] = \frac{(rt)^k}{k!}e^{-rt}\). In a short interval \(dt\) the probability of one event is \(r\,dt\) and of two or more is \(O(dt^2)\). Rates are not probabilities: they have dimensions of inverse time and can exceed \(1\).



2.4.1 The birth–death master equation
Let \(P_n(t)\) be the probability of having \(n\) individuals at time \(t\). With birth and death rates \[W^+(n) = T(n \to n + 1), \qquad W^-(n) = T(n \to n - 1),\] the probability balance over \(dt\) gives the master equation \[\frac{dP_n}{dt} = W^+(n - 1)P_{n-1} + W^-(n + 1)P_{n+1} - \bigl[W^+(n) + W^-(n)\bigr]P_n ,\] a gain–loss equation: the first two terms bring probability into state \(n\), the last takes it out. More generally, for a process with transition rates \(W_{n'n}\) from \(n\) to \(n'\), \[\frac{dP_n}{dt} = \sum_{n'}\bigl[W_{nn'}P_{n'} - W_{n'n}P_n\bigr].\]
A logistic population with immigration has \[W^+(n) = bn + m, \qquad W^-(n) = d(n)\,n = \frac{b}{K}n^2 .\] Births are multiplicative (\(\propto n\)) plus an immigration rate \(m\) that removes the absorbing state \(n = 0\). Deaths increase with crowding. The deterministic limit, \(\dot{\bar n} = W^+(\bar n) - W^-(\bar n) = b\bar n(1 - \bar n/K) + m\), recovers the logistic law.


2.4.2 Probability current and stationary solutions
Write the one-step master equation as a discrete continuity equation, \(\dot P_n = J_{n-1} - J_n\), with the probability current between \(n\) and \(n + 1\) \[J_n = W^+(n)P_n - W^-(n + 1)P_{n+1}.\] At stationarity all \(J_n\) are equal. With a reflecting boundary at \(n = 0\) (\(W^-(0) = 0\)), \(J_{-1} = 0\), so every current vanishes: \(J_n^* = 0\). This is detailed balance, \(W^+(n)P_n^* = W^-(n + 1)P^*_{n+1}\), which can be iterated: \[P_n^* = P_0^*\prod_{z=1}^{n}\frac{W^+(z - 1)}{W^-(z)}, \qquad P_0^* = \Bigl[1 + \sum_{n\geq1}\prod_{z=1}^n\frac{W^+(z - 1)}{W^-(z)}\Bigr]^{-1}.\] Every one-step process with reflecting boundaries satisfies detailed balance at stationarity. Processes with several variables generally do not, and then stationary states carry non-zero probability currents (a hallmark of non-equilibrium systems, Chapter 15).

For \(W^+(n) = bn + m\), \(W^-(n) = bn^2/K\), \[P^*_n = P^*_0\,\frac{\Gamma(n + m/b)}{\Gamma(m/b)}\,\frac{K^n}{(n!)^2} \;\underset{m \ll b}{\simeq}\; P^*_0\,\frac{m}{b}\,\frac{K^n}{n\,n!} \quad (n \geq 1).\]

Proof. \(\prod_{z=1}^n W^+(z-1) = b^n\,\Gamma(n + m/b)/\Gamma(m/b)\) and \(\prod_{z=1}^n W^-(z) = (b/K)^n(n!)^2\). For small \(m/b\), \(\Gamma(n + \varepsilon)/\Gamma(\varepsilon) \simeq \varepsilon(n-1)!\). \(\square\)
The distribution \(K^n/(n\,n!)\) is peaked near \(n \simeq K\) with width \(\simeq\sqrt K\). Unlike the deterministic model, the population can exceed the carrying capacity: for \(K = 50\), \(b = 1\), \(m = 0.1\), the mean is \(49.1\), the standard deviation \(7.1\), and \(P(n > K) \simeq 0.41\).


2.4.3 Moments and the failure of mean-field closure
Multiplying the master equation by \(n\) and summing, \[\frac{d\langle n\rangle}{dt} = \langle W^+(n) - W^-(n)\rangle = b\langle n\rangle + m - \frac bK\langle n^2\rangle .\] Because the death rate is nonlinear, the mean depends on the second moment, the second moment on the third, and so on. The deterministic equation is recovered only by the mean-field approximation \(\langle n^2\rangle \simeq \langle n\rangle^2\), which neglects fluctuations, \(\langle n^2\rangle - \langle n\rangle^2 = O(K)\). Their relative size \(O(K^{-1/2})\) vanishes for large systems. This is the first instance of the system-size expansion developed below and in Chapter 5.


2.4.4 The Gillespie algorithm
Master equations are rarely solvable, but they can be sampled exactly. Consider reactions \(j = 1, \dots, M\) with propensities \(a_j(\mathbf x)\) (rates in state \(\mathbf x\)) and state changes \(\mathbf v_j\), and let \(a_0 = \sum_ja_j\). The probability that nothing happens in \([t, t + \tau]\) satisfies \(P_0(\tau + d\tau) = P_0(\tau)(1 - a_0d\tau)\), so \(P_0(\tau) = e^{-a_0\tau}\). The probability that the next event is reaction \(j\), occurring in \([t + \tau, t + \tau + d\tau]\), is therefore \[P(\tau, j)\,d\tau = a_j\,e^{-a_0\tau}\,d\tau = \underbrace{a_0e^{-a_0\tau}d\tau}_{\text{when}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{a_j}{a_0}}_{\text{which}} .\] The waiting time and the identity of the reaction are independent.


Initialise \(\mathbf x(0)\) and \(t = 0\).
Compute all propensities \(a_j(\mathbf x)\) and \(a_0 = \sum_ja_j\).
Draw the waiting time \(\tau \sim \mathrm{Exp}(a_0)\), e.g. \(\tau = -\ln u_1/a_0\) with \(u_1\) uniform on \((0, 1)\).
Draw \(u_2\) uniform and choose the smallest \(j\) with \(\sum_{k\leq j}a_k > u_2a_0\).
Update \(t \to t + \tau\), \(\mathbf x \to \mathbf x + \mathbf v_j\), and return to step 2.


Each trajectory is an exact sample of the process described by the master equation. Averaging many trajectories reconstructs \(P_n(t)\). For the logistic process with \(K = 50\), starting from \(n = 5\), the average of \(300\) trajectories at \(t = 2, 4, 8\) is \(22.0\), \(40.8\), \(48.4\), against the deterministic \(22.5\), \(42.9\), \(49.9\). The stochastic mean lags slightly behind and saturates slightly below \(K\), as predicted by the moment equation (the \(\langle n^2\rangle\) term exceeds \(\langle n\rangle^2\)).

In a population of \(N\) individuals, \(I\) infected and \(S = N - I\) susceptible, infected individuals recover at rate \(\mu\) (\(I \to S\)) and infect susceptibles on contact (\(I + S \xrightarrow{\lambda} 2I\)). The rates are \[W^-(I) = \mu I, \qquad W^+(I) = \lambda\frac{I(N - I)}{N}.\] \(I = 0\) is absorbing, so \(P(I, t) \to \delta_{I,0}\) as \(t \to \infty\). Yet for \(\lambda > \mu\) the deterministic dynamics has an endemic equilibrium \(I^* = N(1 - \mu/\lambda)\). The stochastic system sits there for a time that grows exponentially with \(N\) before fluctuations drive it to extinction: a metastable (quasi-stationary) state, the relevant one in practice.

section: 2.5 From master equation to Fokker–Planck and Langevin
text:
2.5 From master equation to Fokker–Planck and Langevin

2.5.1 The continuum limit
When populations are large, let \(\Omega\) be a system size (the carrying capacity \(K\), the total population \(N\)) and \(x = n/\Omega\) a density, which becomes continuous as \(\Omega \to \infty\). For rates of the form \(W^\pm(n) = \Omega\,w^\pm(x)\) and \(P_n(t) = P(x, t)/\Omega\), the master equation reads \[\partial_tP(x, t) = \Omega\bigl[(\mathbb E^- - 1)\,w^+(x)P(x, t) + (\mathbb E^+ - 1)\,w^-(x)P(x, t)\bigr],\] with the shift operators \(\mathbb E^\pm f(x) = f(x \pm 1/\Omega)\). Expanding \(\mathbb E^\pm - 1 = \pm\frac1\Omega\partial_x + \frac1{2\Omega^2}\partial_x^2 + \dots\) (Kramers–Moyal expansion) and truncating at second order gives the Fokker–Planck equation \[\partial_tP = -\partial_x\bigl[A(x)P\bigr] + \frac12\partial_x^2\bigl[B(x)P\bigr], \qquad A = w^+ - w^-, \quad B = \frac{w^+ + w^-}{\Omega}.\] The drift \(A\) is the deterministic law. The diffusion \(B\) is small, \(O(1/\Omega)\), and measures demographic noise. Births and deaths both add to it: noise comes from the total event rate, not the net one.
For the stochastic logistic (\(\Omega = K\), \(m = 0\)), \(w^+ = bx\) and \(w^- = bx^2\): \[A(x) = bx(1 - x), \qquad B(x) = \frac bK\,x(1 + x).\] With immigration, \(A = b\bigl[x(1 - x) + \frac m{bK}\bigr]\) and \(B = \frac b{K^2}\bigl[Kx(1 + x) + \frac mb\bigr]\), which no longer vanishes at \(x = 0\): immigration removes the absorbing state.


2.5.2 The Langevin equation
The same process can be described by a stochastic differential equation for a single trajectory, \[\dot x = A(x) + \sqrt{B(x)}\,\xi(t), \qquad \langle\xi(t)\rangle = 0, \quad \langle\xi(t)\xi(t')\rangle = \delta(t - t'),\] whose ensemble of solutions has density \(P(x, t)\) obeying the Fokker–Planck equation (in the Itô interpretation). For the logistic case \[\dot x = bx(1 - x) + \sqrt{\frac{bx(1 + x)}{K}}\;\xi(t).\] The noise amplitude depends on the state: it is multiplicative noise. Numerically, the Euler–Maruyama scheme \[x_{t + \Delta t} = x_t + A(x_t)\Delta t + \sqrt{B(x_t)\,\Delta t}\;\eta_t, \qquad \eta_t \sim \mathcal N(0, 1),\] evaluates the noise amplitude at the beginning of the step (Itô). Evaluating it at the midpoint gives the Stratonovich interpretation, which corresponds to a different Fokker–Planck equation with an extra “noise-induced drift” \(\frac14B'(x)\). This is the Itô–Stratonovich dilemma: for multiplicative white noise the equation alone is ambiguous, and the interpretation is part of the model. Equations derived from master equations, like ours, are Itô.


2.5.3 Random walk and diffusion
The symmetric random walk, \(W^\pm(n) = \lambda\), is the simplest case. With \(x = n\,\Delta x\), \[\partial_tP(x, t) = \lambda\bigl[P(x - \Delta x) + P(x + \Delta x) - 2P(x)\bigr] \simeq \lambda\,\Delta x^2\,\partial_x^2P,\] the diffusion equation \(\partial_tP = D\,\partial_x^2P\), provided \(\lambda \to \infty\) and \(\Delta x \to 0\) with \(D = \lambda\,\Delta x^2\) fixed. Its Langevin form is \(\dot x = \sqrt{2D}\,\xi(t)\), with Gaussian propagator \(P(x, t) = (4\pi Dt)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/4Dt}\).


2.5.4 Stationary solutions of the Fokker–Planck equation
Writing Fokker–Planck as a continuity equation, \(\partial_tP = -\partial_xJ\), with current \(J = AP - \frac12\partial_x(BP)\), a stationary state has constant \(J\). With a reflecting boundary \(J = 0\) everywhere, so \(\partial_x(BP) = 2A\,P\), which integrates to \[P^*(x) = \frac{\mathcal N}{B(x)}\exp\Bigl(2\int^x\frac{A(y)}{B(y)}\,dy\Bigr).\]

For linear rates \(W^+(n) = bn + m\), \(W^-(n) = dn\) with \(d > b\) (decline compensated by immigration), work directly with \(n\): \(A(n) = m - (d - b)n\), \(B(n) \simeq (b + d)n\). Then \[P^*(n) \propto n^{\frac{2m}{b + d} - 1}\,e^{-\frac{2(d - b)}{b + d}\,n},\] a Gamma distribution. The exact discrete solution of the master equation is the negative binomial \[P^*_n = \frac{\Gamma(n + m/b)}{\Gamma(m/b)\,n!}\Bigl(\frac bd\Bigr)^n\Bigl(1 - \frac bd\Bigr)^{m/b},\] whose continuum limit is a Gamma distribution with shape \(m/b\) and rate \(1 - b/d\). The two agree when \(b \simeq d\), the regime where diffusion is accurate.

Proof. With \(A/B = \frac{m}{(b+d)n} - \frac{d - b}{b + d}\), \(2\int A/B = \frac{2m}{b+d}\ln n - \frac{2(d - b)}{b + d}n\), and dividing by \(B \propto n\) gives the result. The discrete one follows from the product formula with \(W^+(z - 1)/W^-(z) = (b(z-1) + m)/(dz)\). \(\square\)
The negative binomial is the cornerstone of neutral theory (Chapter 3). There, each species follows exactly this linear birth–death–immigration process, and the near-critical case \(b \to d\) produces the log-series of species abundances.

section: 2.6 Stochastic doubling and the timing of division
text:
2.6 Stochastic doubling and the timing of division
So far each cell divided at a constant rate. Real E. coli cells grow exponentially in size, \(x(t) = x_0e^{\alpha t}\), and divide at a size \(x_f\) that varies from generation to generation (Osella et al., 2014). Division can be modelled as a random event with a hazard rate \(h_d(x, t)\): the probability of dividing in \([t, t + dt]\), given no division so far, is \(h_d\,dt\).
Let \(P_0(t \mid x_0)\) be the probability that a cell born with size \(x_0\) has not divided by time \(t\) (the survival function). Not dividing up to \(t + dt\) means not dividing up to \(t\) and then not in \([t, t + dt]\): \[P_0(t + dt) = P_0(t)\bigl[1 - h_d(x(t), t)\,dt\bigr] \;\Longrightarrow\; P_0(t \mid x_0) = \exp\Bigl(-\int_0^t h_d(x(s), s)\,ds\Bigr).\] The distribution of division times is then \[P(t \mid x_0) = h_d\bigl(x(t), t\bigr)P_0(t \mid x_0) = -\frac{d}{dt}P_0(t \mid x_0).\] Because size grows monotonically, the same can be written in terms of size, with \(h^*_d(x)\,dx = h_d\,dt\) and \(dx/dt = \alpha x\): \[P(x_f \mid x_0) = h^*_d(x_f)\exp\Bigl(-\int_{x_0}^{x_f}h_d^*(s)\,ds\Bigr).\] The functional form of \(h_d\) distinguishes the classical models of cell-size control:

a timer (\(h_d\) depends on time since birth only),
a sizer (\(h^*_d\) depends on current size only),
an adder (\(h^*_d\) depends on the size added since birth, \(x - x_0\)).

The data favour a “concerted” control, close to the adder, which makes the added size \(x_f - x_0\) independent of \(x_0\) and keeps the size distribution stable over generations. A constant hazard gives back exponentially distributed division times: the Poisson birth process of the master equation.

2.7 Exercises

(HW 1.1) Linear stability. (a) Perform the linear stability analysis of the logistic equation. (b) Do the same for the consumer–resource model with abiotic resource, \(\dot N = (\gamma qR - d)N\), \(\dot R = C - qRN\).


Solution. 

\(F(N) = \mu N(1 - N/K)\), \(F'(N) = \mu(1 - 2N/K)\). \(N^* = 0\): \(F' = \mu > 0\), unstable. \(N^* = K\): \(F' = -\mu < 0\), stable, with relaxation time \(1/\mu\).
The interior equilibrium is \(R^* = d/(\gamma q)\), \(N^* = \gamma C/d\). The Jacobian there is \[J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \gamma qN^* \\ -qR^* & -qN^* \end{pmatrix},\] with \(\operatorname{tr}J = -qN^* < 0\) and \(\det J = \gamma q^2R^*N^* = qC > 0\). Both eigenvalues have negative real part, so the equilibrium is stable. It is a stable node if \((\operatorname{tr}J)^2 > 4\det J\), i.e. \(q^2N^{*2} > 4qC\), which reads \(q\gamma^2C/d^2 > 4\). Otherwise it is a stable focus, approached through damped oscillations. With the numbers of HW 1.2, \(q\gamma^2C/d^2 = 0.2\times0.64\times5/0.16 = 4\): the system sits exactly at the boundary.



(HW 1.2) The QSA in the abiotic case. Apply the QSA to the abiotic consumer–resource model with linear uptake. Check the analytical result with simulations, e.g. with \(\gamma = 0.8\), \(q = 0.2\), \(C = 5\), \(d = 0.4\). How does the solution change with Monod uptake (\(q_M = 3\), \(K_M = 8\))?


Solution. QSA: \(\dot R = 0\) gives \(R = C/(qN)\); then \(\dot N = (\gamma qC/(qN) - d)N = \gamma C - dN\), so \(N(t) = N^* + (N_0 - N^*)e^{-dt}\) with \(N^* = \gamma C/d = 10\), and \(R^* = C/(qN^*) = d/(\gamma q) = 2.5\). Simulating the full system from, e.g., \(N_0 = 1\), \(R_0 = 0\), the population relaxes to \(10\) and the resource to \(2.5\). The match improves the faster the resource relaxes (large \(qN\)). With Monod uptake, QSA gives \(g(R)N = C\) and again \(\dot N = \gamma C - dN\): the same \(N^* = 10\). Only the resource level changes, \(R^* = K_Md/(\gamma q_M - d) = 8 \times 0.4/2 = 1.6\). With Monod the QSA fails when \(N < C/q_M = 5/3\): the cells cannot take up all the supply and \(R\) accumulates, so early transients from small \(N_0\) differ from the QSA prediction.


(HW 1.3, optional) Stochastic versus deterministic logistic growth. Simulate the birth–death process with \(W^+ = bn + m\), \(W^- = bn^2/K\) (\(K = 50\), \(b = 1\), \(m = 0.1\)) with the Gillespie algorithm and compare the mean trajectory with the deterministic solution. Compare the long-time histogram with the exact stationary distribution.


Solution. Averaging \(300\) trajectories from \(n_0 = 5\): \(\langle n\rangle = 22.0\), \(40.8\), \(48.4\), \(49.1\) at \(t = 2, 4, 8, 20\), against the deterministic \(22.5\), \(42.9\), \(49.9\), \(50.0\). The stochastic mean is slightly lower because \(\frac{d\langle n\rangle}{dt}\) involves \(\langle n^2\rangle > \langle n\rangle^2\), which enhances death. At long times the histogram matches \(P_n^* \propto \frac{\Gamma(n + m/b)}{(n!)^2}K^n\): mean \(49.1\), standard deviation \(7.1 \approx \sqrt K\), and \(41\%\) of the time \(n > K\). Individual trajectories fluctuate by \(O(\sqrt K)\) around \(K\), while the deterministic solution sits exactly at \(K\).


(Detailed balance) Show that for any one-step process on \(\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\) with \(W^-(0) = 0\), the stationary currents \(J_n = W^+(n)P_n - W^-(n+1)P_{n+1}\) vanish. Why does this fail for the symmetric random walk on a ring of \(L\) sites with a bias (\(W^+ \neq W^-\))?


Solution. At stationarity \(\dot P_n = J_{n-1} - J_n = 0\), so \(J_n\) is independent of \(n\). At the boundary \(J_{-1} = 0\) (nothing flows below \(0\)), hence all \(J_n = 0\). On a ring there is no boundary: the stationary state is uniform, \(P_n = 1/L\), and carries a constant current \(J = (W^+ - W^-)/L \neq 0\). It is a non-equilibrium steady state, which does not satisfy detailed balance.


(Linear birth–death–immigration) For \(W^+(n) = bn + m\), \(W^-(n) = dn\), \(d > b\): (a) find the stationary distribution from the product formula; (b) compute its mean and compare with the deterministic equilibrium; (c) what happens as \(b \to d\)?


Solution. 

\(P_n^* = P_0^*\prod_{z=1}^n\frac{b(z-1) + m}{dz} = P_0^*\frac{\Gamma(n + m/b)}{\Gamma(m/b)\,n!}\bigl(\frac bd\bigr)^n\), a negative binomial with \(P_0^* = (1 - b/d)^{m/b}\). (b) Its mean is \(\frac{m/b\cdot b/d}{1 - b/d} = \frac{m}{d - b}\), equal to the deterministic equilibrium of \(\dot n = m - (d - b)n\): for linear rates the mean obeys the deterministic equation exactly. (c) As \(b \to d\) the mean diverges and the distribution develops a long tail \(P_n \propto n^{m/b - 1}(b/d)^n\). For \(m/b \to 0\) this is \(\propto x^n/n\), Fisher’s log-series (Chapter 3).



(Fokker–Planck coefficients) For the logistic process with immigration, derive \(A(x)\) and \(B(x)\) by the Kramers–Moyal expansion and write the associated Langevin equation. Show that \(x = 0\) is no longer absorbing.


Solution. With \(x = n/K\): \(w^+(x) = W^+/K = bx + m/K\) and \(w^-(x) = W^-/K = bx^2\). Then \(A = w^+ - w^- = b\bigl(x(1 - x) + \frac m{bK}\bigr)\) and \(B = (w^+ + w^-)/K = \frac b{K^2}\bigl(Kx(1 + x) + \frac mb\bigr)\). The Langevin equation is \(\dot x = A(x) + \sqrt{B(x)}\,\xi\). At \(x = 0\): \(A(0) = m/K > 0\) and \(B(0) = m/K^2 > 0\), so the drift pushes the population away from zero. Without immigration \(A(0) = B(0) = 0\) and extinction is permanent.


(Division with constant hazard) (a) If \(h_d = k\) is constant, find the distribution of division times and its mean. (b) For a sizer with \(h^*_d(x) = \kappa(x - x_c)^2\) for \(x > x_c\) (\(0\) otherwise), and exponential growth from \(x_0 < x_c\), find \(P(x_f \mid x_0)\) and explain why it does not depend on \(x_0\).


Solution. 

\(P_0(t) = e^{-kt}\) and \(P(t) = ke^{-kt}\), exponential with mean \(1/k\): memoryless division, as in the birth process. (b) \(P_0(x_f) = \exp\bigl(-\int_{x_c}^{x_f}\kappa(s - x_c)^2ds\bigr) = e^{-\kappa(x_f - x_c)^3/3}\), so \(P(x_f) = \kappa(x_f - x_c)^2e^{-\kappa(x_f - x_c)^3/3}\) for \(x_f > x_c\), a Weibull distribution. Because the hazard is zero below \(x_c\), the birth size only shifts when \(x_c\) is reached, not the distribution of division sizes. This is the defining property of a sizer: the final size carries no memory of the initial one. An adder instead gives \(x_f - x_0\) independent of \(x_0\).

title: 3  Many species: neutral theory and upscaling
text:
3.1 Species abundance distributions
From one population we move to communities of hundreds or thousands of species, such as the trees of a tropical forest. Writing a model with species-specific parameters for each of them is hopeless. Yet community-level patterns, above all the distribution of species abundances, are remarkably regular. This chapter shows that a minimal model, in which every species obeys the same stochastic birth–death dynamics (neutral theory), predicts these patterns. Its solution, the negative binomial distribution, has a scaling property that lets us infer the biodiversity of a whole forest from a small sample. Real forests turn out to sit close to a critical point of the model.
A census of a plot records the abundance \(n_i\) of every species \(i = 1, \dots, S\). Two equivalent summaries are used:
Empirical RSAs are dominated by rare species: many species have one or two individuals, and a few are hyper-abundant. Plotted on a linear scale they are hollow curves with very sparse tails. Ecologists therefore use Preston plots, which group abundances into octaves \([2^k, 2^{k+1})\) and plot the number of species per octave against \(k = \log_2 n\).

title: 3  Many species: neutral theory and upscaling
text:
the relative species abundance (RSA) \(\phi_n\): the number of species with exactly \(n\) individuals;
the species abundance distribution (SAD) \(P(n) = \phi_n/S\): the probability that a randomly chosen species has \(n\) individuals.








WarningBe careful with binning



An octave collects many more abundance values at large \(k\) than at small \(k\). The count in octave \(k\) is \(\sum_{n=2^k}^{2^{k+1}-1}\phi_n \simeq 2^k\phi_{2^k}\ln2\), which is \(n\,\phi_n\) rather than \(\phi_n\). A log-series \(\phi_n = \theta x^n/n\), monotonically decreasing in \(n\), therefore looks flat per octave (each octave holds about \(\theta\ln2\) species) up to \(n \sim 1/(1 - x)\), and then drops. A genuine interior maximum in a Preston plot indicates that \(n\phi_n\) increases, which the log-series cannot produce but a negative binomial with \(r > 1\) can. Always state the binning before interpreting a shape.

title: 3  Many species: neutral theory and upscaling
section: 3.2 From individual dynamics to the negative binomial
text:
3.2 From individual dynamics to the negative binomial

3.2.1 Density-dependent birth and death
Let \(P^s_n(t)\) be the probability that species \(s\) has \(n\) individuals. If each species follows a one-step process with rates \(b^s_n\) and \(d^s_n\), the master equation is \[\frac{dP^s_n}{dt} = b^s_{n-1}P^s_{n-1} + d^s_{n+1}P^s_{n+1} - (b^s_n + d^s_n)P^s_n .\] The per-capita rates may depend on abundance. Expanding them for large \(n\), \[\frac{b^s_n}{n} = b_s + \frac{r_s}{n} + O(n^{-2}), \qquad \frac{d^s_n}{n} = d_s + \frac{d_1}{n} + O(n^{-2}).\] Such density dependence is observed: seedlings close to adults of the same species suffer more from specialised pests (the Janzen–Connell effect), so being rare is an advantage. The simplest choice keeping the leading terms is \[b^s_n = b_sn + r_s, \qquad d^s_n = d_sn,\] exactly the linear birth–death–immigration process of Chapter 2. The constant \(r_s\) plays the role of immigration (or speciation) and keeps rare species from going extinct.
Treating each species independently amounts to replacing the joint distribution \(P(n_1, \dots, n_S)\) by a product \(\prod_sP^s(n_s)\): interactions are absorbed into effective, mean-field rates.


3.2.2 The stationary solution
By the product formula of Chapter 2, \[P^{s*}_n = P^{s*}_0\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{b_{j-1}}{d_j} = P^{s*}_0\,\frac{\Gamma(n + r)}{\Gamma(r)\,n!}\,\xi^n, \qquad \xi = \frac bd, \quad r = \frac{r_s}{b_s},\] dropping the label \(s\). This is the negative binomial distribution \[P^{\mathrm{NB}}_n(r, \xi) = \binom{n + r - 1}{n}\xi^n(1 - \xi)^r, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots,\] which requires \(\xi < 1\) (deaths outweigh births) and \(r > 0\). Its generating function is particularly simple: \[G(z) = \sum_{n\geq0}P^{\mathrm{NB}}_nz^n = \Bigl(\frac{1 - \xi}{1 - \xi z}\Bigr)^r,\] from which the mean \(\langle n\rangle = G'(1) = \frac{r\xi}{1 - \xi}\) and the variance \(\frac{r\xi}{(1 - \xi)^2}\) follow. In a census only species that are present are counted, so the RSA is the NB truncated to \(n \geq 1\): \[P^*_n(r, \xi) = \frac{1}{1 - (1 - \xi)^r}\binom{n + r - 1}{n}\xi^n(1 - \xi)^r, \qquad n \geq 1 .\]

As \(r \to 0\) the truncated NB tends to Fisher’s log-series \[P^*_n \to \frac{1}{-\ln(1 - \xi)}\,\frac{\xi^n}{n}.\]

Proof. \(\binom{n + r - 1}{n} = \frac{r(r + 1)\cdots(r + n - 1)}{n!} \simeq \frac{r\,(n - 1)!}{n!} = \frac rn\) and \(1 - (1 - \xi)^r \simeq -r\ln(1 - \xi)\) as \(r \to 0\). \(\square\)

title: 3  Many species: neutral theory and upscaling
text:
3.3 Neutral theory

3.3.1 The neutrality hypothesis
Fitting species-specific \((r_s, \xi_s)\) to thousands of species would need thousands of parameters. Hubbell’s neutral theory (2001) assumes instead that species on the same trophic level (e.g. all tree species of a forest) are demographically equivalent: they have the same per-capita birth, death, dispersal and speciation rates. Different species are then different realisations of the same stochastic process, and their abundances differ only by chance (ecological drift), not by fitness.
Under neutrality the \(S\) species are \(S\) independent draws from one distribution, so the expected RSA is simply \(\phi_n = S\,P^*_n(r, \xi)\), with two parameters for the whole community. Fits of the NB to the RSA of large tropical forest plots (Barro Colorado Island, Pasoh, Korup, Lambir, Yasuní, Sinharaja) are excellent. Neutrality is surprising, since species obviously differ, and controversial. Its success says that, for the abundance distribution, differences between species average out in very diverse communities. It is a null model, and departures from it point to the biology that matters.


3.3.2 The voter model with speciation
Neutral theory can also be formulated in a spatially explicit, zero-sum way. A landscape (say, a lattice) is saturated by \(J\) individuals. At each step a random individual dies and is replaced either by the offspring of a neighbour (probability \(1 - \nu\)) or by an individual of a brand-new species (speciation, probability \(\nu\)). Without speciation this is the voter model of statistical physics: domains of the same “opinion” coarsen and one species eventually takes over. Speciation injects diversity and produces a statistically stationary community.
In the well-mixed (mean-field) version, the abundance of each species performs a birth–death walk with \(b \lesssim d\), and new species enter at rate \(\nu\). The resulting metacommunity RSA is the log-series \[\langle\phi_n\rangle = \theta\,\frac{x^n}{n}, \qquad \theta \simeq \frac{2J\nu}{1 - \nu},\] where \(\theta\) is Hubbell’s fundamental biodiversity number and \(x = b/d \to 1\) for large communities. The mean number of species found among \(J\) individuals is \(\langle S\rangle = \theta\ln(1 + J/\theta)\) (Ewens’ sampling formula).


3.3.3 A local community fed by a metacommunity
Real plots are open: they receive immigrants from a large surrounding metacommunity, the “continent” to the plot’s “island”. Consider an island of fixed size \(J\) (zero-sum dynamics). At each event an individual dies, and the vacancy is filled with probability \(1 - m\) by local reproduction and with probability \(m\) by an immigrant drawn from the metacommunity, where species \(k\) has relative abundance \(\mu_k/J_M\). The rates for species \(k\) with \(n\) individuals on the island are \[b_{n,k} = (1 - m)\Bigl(1 - \frac nJ\Bigr)\frac{n}{J - 1} + m\Bigl(1 - \frac nJ\Bigr)\frac{\mu_k}{J_M},\] \[d_{n,k} = (1 - m)\frac nJ\,\frac{J - n}{J - 1} + m\,\frac nJ\Bigl(1 - \frac{\mu_k}{J_M}\Bigr).\] In \(b_{n,k}\) an individual of another species dies (probability \(1 - n/J\)) and is replaced by a local offspring of \(k\) or by an immigrant of \(k\). In \(d_{n,k}\) an individual of \(k\) dies and is replaced by another species. With \[\lambda_k = \frac{m}{1 - m}(J - 1)\frac{\mu_k}{J_M}, \qquad \theta_k = J + \frac{m}{1 - m}(J - 1)\Bigl(1 - \frac{\mu_k}{J_M}\Bigr),\] the rates become \(b_{n,k} = \frac{1 - m}{J}\frac{J - n}{J - 1}(n + \lambda_k)\) and \(d_{n,k} = \frac{1 - m}{J - 1}\frac nJ(\theta_k - n)\), and the stationary distribution is \[P^*_{n,k} = P_{0,k}\,\frac{J!}{n!\,(J - n)!}\,\frac{\Gamma(n + \lambda_k)}{\Gamma(\lambda_k)}\,\frac{\Gamma(\theta_k - n)}{\Gamma(\theta_k)} .\] On a log scale it resembles a log-normal, but it comes from a mechanism, which is why Volkov et al. (2003) prefer it to the phenomenological log-normal. The island RSA follows by averaging over the metacommunity abundances, \(\phi_n = S_M\sum_kP^*_{n,k}P(\mu_k)\). Strong dispersal limitation (small \(m\)) depletes rare species locally and produces the hump of empirical Preston plots.

title: 3  Many species: neutral theory and upscaling
section: 3.4 Upscaling: from a sample to the whole forest
text:
3.4 Upscaling: from a sample to the whole forest

3.4.1 The problem
The Amazon holds about \(10^{11}\) trees; no census can count them. Typically, plots covering a fraction \(p = a/A \ll 1\) of a forest of area \(A\) are sampled. How many species does the whole forest contain? Rare species are mostly missed by small samples, so the RSA is scale dependent. At small \(p\) it is a hollow curve dominated by singletons. At larger \(p\), species accumulate individuals, mass moves out of the lowest abundance classes, and the curve develops an interior maximum. Linear extrapolation of \(S\) fails.


3.4.2 Binomial sampling and self-similarity
Assume individuals are spread over the forest independently of each other (random placement, or well-mixed). If a species has \(n\) individuals in total, the number \(k\) found in a region covering a fraction \(p\) of the area is binomial: \[P_p(k \mid n) = \binom nkp^k(1 - p)^{n - k}.\] The abundance distribution at scale \(p\) is then \[P_p(k) = \sum_{n\geq k}\binom nkp^k(1 - p)^{n-k}\,P_n(r, \xi).\]

If abundances at scale \(1\) are \(\mathrm{NB}(r, \xi)\), then abundances at scale \(p\) are \(\mathrm{NB}(r, \xi_p)\) with the same \(r\) and \[\xi_p = \frac{p\,\xi}{1 - \xi(1 - p)} .\]

Proof. Binomial thinning acts on generating functions as \(G_p(z) = G(1 - p + pz)\): each individual is kept with probability \(p\). For the NB, \[G_p(z) = \Bigl(\frac{1 - \xi}{1 - \xi + \xi p - \xi pz}\Bigr)^r = \Bigl(\frac{1 - \xi_p}{1 - \xi_pz}\Bigr)^r, \qquad 1 - \xi_p = \frac{1 - \xi}{1 - \xi(1 - p)},\] again an NB, with \(\xi_p\) as stated. \(\square\)
The NB is a fixed form under coarse-graining, like a renormalisation-group fixed point: only \(\xi\) flows with scale, \(r\) does not. Inverting, \[\xi = \frac{\xi_p}{p + \xi_p(1 - p)} .\]


3.4.3 Estimating the number of species
A species is missed by the sample with probability \(P_p(0)\). If \(S^*\) species are observed at scale \(p\), then \(S^* = S\,[1 - P_p(0)]\). For the NB truncated at scale \(1\), \(P_p(0) = \frac{(1 - \xi_p)^r - (1 - \xi)^r}{1 - (1 - \xi)^r}\), hence \[S = S^*\,\frac{1 - (1 - \xi)^r}{1 - (1 - \xi_p)^r}.\] The recipe: fit a truncated NB to the sample RSA to get \((r, \xi_p)\); compute \(\xi\) from self-similarity; compute \(S\). The same machinery predicts the RSA and the species–area relationship at any scale \(p' \in (p, 1]\).
The method was validated on computer-generated forests, where the truth is known, and on fully censused plots sub-sampled at random. It outperforms classical estimators based on the log-series or on non-parametric corrections (Chao). Applied to tropical forests (Tovo et al., 2017), it predicts, for instance, about \(366 \pm 15\) tree species at Barro Colorado from \(301\) observed, and an Amazonian richness of order \(10^4\) species. The large number of hyper-rare species implied (hyper-rarity), together with the dominance of a few hundred species (hyper-dominance), is the main ecological outcome.


3.4.4 How much data is enough?
A bootstrap answers whether a sample is large enough. Upscale the sample from \(p^*\) to \(1\) (estimate \(S\)); generate synthetic samples at a scale \(p_{\text{pred}}\) by binomial thinning; upscale them again and compare the new estimate \(S'\) with \(S\). The smallest \(p_{\text{pred}}\) for which \(S' \simeq S\) within the desired precision is the scale that encodes sufficient information. If \(p_{\text{pred}}/p^* > 1\) more fieldwork is needed; if it is below \(1\) the sample is more than sufficient.

section: 3.5 Tropical forests are near a critical point
text:
3.5 Tropical forests are near a critical point
The relative fluctuations of a species’ abundance are measured by the coefficient of variation \[\mathrm{CV} = \frac{\sqrt{\langle(n - \langle n\rangle)^2\rangle}}{\langle n\rangle} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{r\,\xi}}\quad \text{(untruncated NB)},\] and for the truncated NB it diverges in the limit \(\xi \to 1\), \(r \to 0\), where the distribution becomes the log-series with a cut-off \(1/(1 - \xi) \to \infty\). In that limit the system has no characteristic abundance scale: births balance deaths (\(b = d\)), the hallmark of a critical point. Fits of \((r, \xi)\) to real forests consistently give \(r \lesssim 1\) and \(\xi\) extremely close to \(1\) (\(\ln(1 - \xi) \sim -10\) to \(-20\)): tropical forests sit very near criticality, with large fluctuations of species abundances across forests.

title: 3  Many species: neutral theory and upscaling
text:
3.6 A phenomenological renormalisation group
Random placement neglects spatial clustering: trees of the same species aggregate because seeds fall near their parents. Clustering is quantified by the pair correlation function \[g(r) = \frac{\langle n_{\mathbf x}\,n_{\mathbf y}\rangle}{\langle n\rangle^2}, \qquad r = |\mathbf x - \mathbf y|,\] where \(n_{\mathbf x}\) is the abundance in a small cell at \(\mathbf x\) and the average runs over positions and, by neutrality, over species. A spatially explicit neutral model with dispersal predicts \[g(r) = 1 + \frac1T\Bigl(\frac\rho\lambda\Bigr)^2K_0\Bigl(\frac r\lambda\Bigr),\] with \(K_0\) the modified Bessel function of the second kind, \(\lambda\) a correlation length set by dispersal and speciation, and \(T\), \(\rho\) model constants. Taking the continuum (Gamma) version of the NB as the RSA in a circle of radius \(R\), \[P(n \mid \alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{\beta\,\Gamma(\alpha)}\Bigl(\frac n\beta\Bigr)^{\alpha - 1}e^{-n/\beta},\] the parameters at each scale are fixed by matching the first two moments, \[\alpha(R) = \frac{\langle N(R)\rangle^2}{\sigma^2(R)}, \qquad \beta(R) = \frac{\sigma^2(R)}{\langle N(R)\rangle},\] with \(\langle N(R)\rangle = \pi R^2\langle n\rangle\) and \(\sigma^2(R)\) obtained by integrating \(g\) over pairs of points in the circle. The flow of \((\alpha, \beta)\) with \(R\) is an empirical renormalisation group: it predicts the RSA, and from it the SAR, at every scale, now including clustering (Azaele et al., 2015).

title: 3  Many species: neutral theory and upscaling
text:
3.7 Biodiversity from presence–absence data
Abundances are expensive to measure; presence/absence on a grid of cells is cheaper. Two summaries replace the RSA:

the relative species occupancy (RSO): the number of species occupying \(c\) cells;
the species accumulation curve (SAC): the mean number of species \(\langle S_a\rangle\) found in randomly placed sub-areas of size \(a < a^*\), with \(a^*\) the surveyed area.

Under the NB model the probability that a species is absent from a cell of relative area \(p\) is \(P_p(0)\), computed above. The expected SAC is therefore \[\langle S_a\rangle = S\bigl[1 - P_{a/A}(0)\bigr],\] a closed form in \((r, \xi, S)\). Fitting it to the empirical SAC inside the surveyed area, and extrapolating to \(a = A\), estimates total biodiversity from presence–absence data alone (Tovo et al., 2019). The fitted parameters also predict the RSO, which provides an independent check.

text:
3.8 Exercises

(Negative binomial from the master equation) For \(b_n = bn + r_s\), \(d_n = dn\), show that the stationary distribution is \(\mathrm{NB}(r, \xi)\) with \(r = r_s/b\), \(\xi = b/d\). Compute its mean and variance from the generating function.


Solution. \(P^*_n = P^*_0\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{b(j - 1) + r_s}{dj} = P^*_0\frac{\xi^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^n(j - 1 + r) = P^*_0\frac{\Gamma(n + r)}{\Gamma(r)\,n!}\xi^n\). Normalisation gives \(P^*_0 = (1 - \xi)^r\) by the binomial series \(\sum_n\binom{n + r - 1}n\xi^n = (1 - \xi)^{-r}\). With \(G(z) = ((1 - \xi)/(1 - \xi z))^r\): \(G'(1) = \frac{r\xi}{1 - \xi}\) and \(G''(1) = \frac{r(r + 1)\xi^2}{(1 - \xi)^2}\), so the variance is \(G'' + G' - G'^2 = \frac{r\xi}{(1 - \xi)^2}\). The variance-to-mean ratio \(1/(1 - \xi) > 1\) makes the distribution over-dispersed compared to a Poisson.


(Preston octaves of a log-series) For \(\phi_n = \theta x^n/n\) with \(x = 0.99\) and \(\theta = 50\), compute the number of species in octaves \(\{1\}, \{2, 3\}, \{4, \dots, 7\}, \dots\). Explain the shape.


Solution. For \(x \to 1\) each octave \(k \geq 1\) contains \(\theta\sum_{n=2^k}^{2^{k+1}-1}1/n \to \theta\ln2 \simeq 34.7\) species. The first octave has \(\theta x = 49.5\), the second \(\theta(x^2/2 + x^3/3) \simeq 40.7\). With \(x = 0.99\) the cut-off \(1/(1 - x) = 100\) makes octaves beyond \(n \sim 100\) (\(k \geq 7\)) decay exponentially. The Preston plot is a plateau followed by a fall, not a hump: a monotone \(\phi_n\) looks flat when binned in octaves.


(Self-similarity) Verify by direct summation, for \(r = 1\), that binomial sampling maps \(\mathrm{NB}(1, \xi)\) (a geometric distribution) into \(\mathrm{NB}(1, \xi_p)\). Then show that \(\xi_p\) decreases monotonically as \(p\) decreases, and interpret.


Solution. \(P_n = (1 - \xi)\xi^n\). \(P_p(k) = \sum_{n\geq k}\binom nkp^k(1 - p)^{n-k}(1 - \xi)\xi^n = (1 - \xi)(p\xi)^k\sum_{m\geq0}\binom{m + k}k[\xi(1 - p)]^m = \frac{(1 - \xi)(p\xi)^k}{[1 - \xi(1 - p)]^{k+1}}\), which is \((1 - \xi_p)\xi_p^k\) with \(\xi_p = \frac{p\xi}{1 - \xi(1 - p)}\). Since \(\frac{d\xi_p}{dp} = \frac{\xi(1 - \xi)}{[1 - \xi(1 - p)]^2} > 0\), smaller samples have smaller \(\xi_p\): the distribution is pushed toward low abundances, giving the hollow curves of small plots.


(Upscaling a forest) The file RSA_sampled_1percent.xlsx contains the abundances of the \(S^* = 4283\) species observed in a \(1\%\) random sample of a forest (total \(39\,779\) individuals). Fit a truncated NB by maximum likelihood, upscale it to \(p = 1\), and estimate the total number of species. Compare with the estimate from Fisher’s log-series, \(S(J) = \theta\ln(1 + J/\theta)\), extrapolated to \(100\) times more individuals.


Solution. Maximising \(\sum_i\ln P^*_{n_i}(r, \xi_p)\) gives \(r = 0.82\) and \(\xi_p = 0.906\). Inverting self-similarity with \(p = 0.01\): \(\xi = \xi_p/(p + \xi_p(1 - p)) = 0.99897\). Then \(S = S^*\frac{1 - (1 - \xi)^r}{1 - (1 - \xi_p)^r} \simeq 4976\). The forest is a computer-generated one with \(4974\) species (Lecture 2), so the NB estimate is essentially exact. The log-series fit to the sample gives \(\theta = 1218\) and, extrapolated to \(100J\) individuals, \(S \simeq 9856\), a twofold overestimate. Fixing \(r = 0\) forces too many rare species.


(Criticality) For the untruncated \(\mathrm{NB}(r, \xi)\) show that \(\mathrm{CV}^2 = 1/(r\xi)\). For the truncated NB with \(r \to 0\) (log-series with parameter \(\xi\)), compute \(\langle n\rangle\) and \(\langle n^2\rangle\) and show that the CV diverges as \(\xi \to 1\).


Solution. Mean \(\frac{r\xi}{1-\xi}\), variance \(\frac{r\xi}{(1-\xi)^2}\), so \(\mathrm{CV}^2 = \frac{1}{r\xi}\). For the log-series \(P_n = \frac{\xi^n}{n\,L}\) with \(L = -\ln(1 - \xi)\): \(\langle n\rangle = \frac{\xi}{(1 - \xi)L}\) and \(\langle n^2\rangle = \frac{\xi}{(1 - \xi)^2L}\). Then \(\mathrm{CV}^2 = \frac{\langle n^2\rangle}{\langle n\rangle^2} - 1 = \frac{L}{\xi} - 1 \simeq -\ln(1 - \xi) \to \infty\). Fluctuations grow without bound as births and deaths balance: the critical point of the neutral model.


(Neutral community simulation) Simulate the mean-field neutral model: a community of \(J = 2000\) individuals; at each step one random individual dies and is replaced with probability \(1 - \nu\) by the offspring of a random individual, and with probability \(\nu\) by a new species. Run to stationarity for \(\nu = 0.005\) and compare the RSA with the log-series \(\theta x^n/n\), \(\theta = 2J\nu/(1 - \nu)\).


Solution. After a transient of order \(J/\nu\) deaths, the number of species fluctuates around Ewens’ \(\langle S\rangle = \sum_{i=0}^{J-1}\frac{\theta}{\theta + i} \simeq \theta\ln(1 + J/\theta)\). With \(\theta \simeq 20.1\) this is about \(93\) species. The time-averaged RSA follows \(\theta x^n/n\), with \(x\) fixed by \(\sum_nn\phi_n = J\). Singletons are the most common abundance class, and a few species hold hundreds of individuals. Many rare species and few dominant ones arise from pure drift, without fitness differences.

title: 4  Spatial and temporal patterns of biodiversity
text:
4.1 Species–area and endemic–area relationships
Chapter 3 explained the distribution of abundances in a community. Ecologists measure several other macroecological patterns: how many species are found in areas of increasing size, how many are endemic to an area, how long species persist before disappearing locally. This chapter derives them from the same null model of independent, randomly placed species. It then shows how space changes the picture, gives a “grand-canonical” formulation in which the number of species itself fluctuates, and closes with metapopulations: species living on a network of habitat patches, whose persistence becomes a spectral problem.

4  Spatial and temporal patterns of biodiversity

title: 4  Spatial and temporal patterns of biodiversity
text:
4.1.1 Three regimes of the SAR
Over many orders of magnitude of area, the SAR has three phases. At small scales \(S\) grows quickly, roughly linearly, because every new individual tends to be a new species. At intermediate scales it grows sublinearly, close to a power law \(S \propto A^z\) with \(z \approx 0.2\)–\(0.3\). At continental scales it steepens again, because new areas contain new, independent biotas. We model the intermediate regime.


4.1.2 The random-placement null model
Following Coleman (1981), divide a region of area \(A\) containing \(S\) species into cells and consider a sub-area \(a\), a fraction \(\alpha = a/A\) of the total. Individuals are placed independently and uniformly (random placement). A species with \(n_i\) individuals is absent from \(a\) with probability \(q_i = (1 - \alpha)^{n_i}\) and present with probability \(p_i = 1 - q_i\). The number of species found in \(a\) is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables, with generating function \[G(z) = \prod_{i=1}^S\bigl(q_i + p_iz\bigr).\] Its mean and variance, given the abundances \(\mathbf n = (n_1, \dots, n_S)\), are \[\langle s(a \mid \mathbf n)\rangle = \sum_ip_i = S - \sum_{i=1}^S(1 - \alpha)^{n_i}, \qquad \sigma^2(a \mid \mathbf n) = \sum_ip_iq_i = \sum_i\bigl[(1 - \alpha)^{n_i} - (1 - \alpha)^{2n_i}\bigr].\] If the abundances themselves are independent draws from the SAD \(P(n)\), averaging over \(\mathbf n\) gives \[\mathrm{SAR}(a) = S\Bigl[1 - \sum_{n\geq1}(1 - \alpha)^nP(n)\Bigr] = S\bigl[1 - \mathcal G(1 - \alpha)\bigr],\] where \(\mathcal G(z) = \sum_nP(n)z^n\) is the generating function of the SAD. The SAR is the SAD’s generating function evaluated at \(1 - \alpha\).


4.1.3 The endemic–area relationship
A species is endemic to \(a\) if all its individuals fall inside \(a\), which happens with probability \(\alpha^{n_i}\). Hence \[\mathrm{EAR}(a \mid \mathbf n) = \sum_i\alpha^{n_i}, \qquad \mathrm{EAR}(a) = S\sum_{n\geq1}\alpha^nP(n) = S\,\mathcal G(\alpha).\]

Under random placement, for any SAD, \[\mathrm{EAR}(a) = S - \mathrm{SAR}(A - a).\]

Proof. \(S - \mathrm{SAR}(A - a) = S\,\mathcal G(1 - (1 - \alpha)) = S\,\mathcal G(\alpha)\). A species is endemic to \(a\) exactly when it is absent from the complement \(A - a\). \(\square\)


4.1.4 The log-series case
For the log-series \(P(n) = \frac{x^n}{n\,|\ln(1 - x)|}\) (with \(x = 1 - \nu\) close to \(1\)), \(\mathcal G(z) = \frac{\ln(1 - xz)}{\ln(1 - x)}\), so \[\frac{\mathrm{SAR}(\alpha)}{S} = 1 - \frac{\ln\bigl(1 - x(1 - \alpha)\bigr)}{\ln(1 - x)} = 1 + \frac{\ln\bigl(\nu(1 - \alpha) + \alpha\bigr)}{|\ln\nu|}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{EAR}(\alpha)}{S} = \frac{\ln(1 - x\alpha)}{\ln(1 - x)}.\] At small \(\alpha\) the SAR grows linearly (\(\simeq \alpha x/[(1 - x)|\ln\nu|]\)); at intermediate \(\alpha\) it grows logarithmically, which over a couple of decades is hard to distinguish from a power law. The EAR stays tiny until \(\alpha\) approaches \(1\) and then shoots up.

Figure: SAR (solid) and EAR (dashed) under random placement with a log-series SAD, \(x = 0.99\).


4.1.5 Habitat loss and extinctions
Destroying a fraction of a region eliminates the species endemic to the destroyed part. The correct estimate of extinctions is therefore \(\mathrm{EAR}(a_{\text{lost}})\), which by the complementarity above equals \(S - \mathrm{SAR}(A - a_{\text{lost}})\). The common practice of fitting a power-law SAR, \(S \propto A^z\), and predicting a loss \(1 - (1 - f)^z\) for a lost fraction \(f\) uses an approximate SAR and typically overestimates extinctions. He and Hubbell (2011) showed that the EAR rises much more slowly than this backward extrapolation of the SAR suggests.

title: 4  Spatial and temporal patterns of biodiversity
text:
4.2 Persistence times

4.2.1 The species persistence-time distribution
Monitoring a region over time, a species appears (by speciation, immigration or recolonisation), persists for a while, and disappears. The species persistence time (SPT) \(\tau\) is the length of such an interval. Breeding-bird surveys in North America, grassland plots in Kansas, fish and forest censuses all give SPT distributions with a power-law body and a cut-off. Long-term data provide many intervals \(\tau_1, \tau_2, \dots\), treated as realisations of the same process, from which the distribution can be estimated.


4.2.2 Mean-field solution by generating functions
Take a species with linear rates \(b_n = bn\), \(d_n = dn\) (no immigration, \(b \lesssim d\)), starting from \(m\) individuals. The generating function \(G(z, t) = \sum_nP_n(t)z^n\) turns the master equation into a first-order PDE. Multiplying by \(z^n\) and summing, \[\frac{\partial G}{\partial t} = \bigl(d + bz^2 - (b + d)z\bigr)\frac{\partial G}{\partial z} = (1 - z)(d - bz)\,\frac{\partial G}{\partial z},\] with \(G(z, 0) = z^m\). It is solved by the method of characteristics. Along curves with \(\frac{dz}{dt} = -(1 - z)(d - bz)\), \(G\) is constant. Integrating by partial fractions with \(\delta = d - b > 0\), \[\frac{(z - 1)\bigl(bz_0 - d\bigr)}{(z_0 - 1)(bz - d)} = e^{-\delta t},\] which gives the initial point \(z_0\) of the characteristic through \((z, t)\): \[z_0 = \frac{d - g}{b - g}, \qquad g(z, t) = e^{-\delta t}\,\frac{bz - d}{z - 1}.\] Hence \(G(z, t) = \bigl[\frac{d - g(z, t)}{b - g(z, t)}\bigr]^m\). The probability of being extinct at time \(t\) is \(P_0(t) = G(0, t)\): \[P_0(t) = \Bigl[\frac{d\,(1 - e^{-\delta t})}{d - b\,e^{-\delta t}}\Bigr]^m.\] For \(m = 1\) the persistence probability \(\mathcal P(t) = 1 - P_0(t)\) is \[\mathcal P(t) = \frac{\delta\,e^{-\delta t}}{d - b\,e^{-\delta t}} \;\simeq\; \frac1{dt}\,\mathcal F(\delta t), \qquad \mathcal F(x) = \frac{x}{e^x - 1},\] in the scaling regime \(\delta \to 0\), \(t \to \infty\) with \(\delta t\) fixed. \(\mathcal F\) is a finite-size scaling function: \(\mathcal F(x) \to 1\) for \(x \to 0\) and decays exponentially for \(x \gg 1\). The SPT density is \[p(\tau) = -\frac{d\mathcal P}{d\tau} \propto \tau^{-2}\,f(\delta\tau),\] a power law with exponent \(2\) and an exponential cut-off at \(\tau_c = 1/\delta = 1/(d - b)\). At criticality (\(b = d\)) the cut-off disappears. The exponent differs from that of the first return of an unbiased random walk (\(3/2\)) because the step rates are proportional to \(n\): large populations fluctuate faster.
If instead \(b > d\), a finite fraction of species never goes extinct; if \(b < d\) with a large gap, lifetimes are exponential with mean \(1/(d - b)\).


4.2.3 Space changes the exponent
The mean-field model ignores space. In the spatial voter model with speciation (Chapter 3), individuals sit on a lattice or network, die, and are replaced by a neighbour’s offspring or, with probability \(\nu\), by a new species. Simulations give power-law SPT distributions whose exponent depends on the geometry. In terms of the cumulative persistence \(\mathcal P(t) \sim t^{-\beta}\):

\(\beta \simeq 1/2\) on a one-dimensional chain (lifetimes \(\propto t^{-3/2}\), as for a random walk),
intermediate values on river-like networks and in two dimensions (where logarithmic corrections appear),
\(\beta \simeq 1\) in three dimensions and in the well-mixed (global) case, recovering the mean-field \(t^{-2}\) density.

Spatial constraints make species persist longer: a species confined to a region of a chain can only be eroded from its edges.


4.2.4 Sampling effects
Observation windows are finite. A species already present at the start, or still present at the end, has a truncated measured lifetime. Censoring piles up probability at the longest observable time and produces a spurious bump at the end of the empirical distribution. Suweis et al. (2012) model the effective lifetime \(L_e\) in terms of the true one \(L\), the observation window \([x_0, x_f]\) and the appearance time, and derive the distribution of \(L_e\). This model fits breeding-bird, grassland, forest and fish data, including the final bump, with the same underlying power-law SPT.

section: 4.3 The grand-canonical formulation of neutral theory
text:
4.3 The grand-canonical formulation of neutral theory
So far the number of individuals was fixed. Let it fluctuate, and describe the community by the occupation numbers \(\boldsymbol\phi = (\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots)\): \(\phi_k\) is the number of species with abundance \(k\). Species are created (speciation or immigration) at rate \(b_0\) with one individual. A species with \(k\) individuals gains one at rate \(b_k\) and loses one at rate \(d_k\), moving from class \(k\) to \(k \pm 1\). Writing \(\hat e_k\) for the unit vector of class \(k\), \[\dot P(\boldsymbol\phi) = b_0P(\boldsymbol\phi - \hat e_1) + d_1(\phi_1 + 1)P(\boldsymbol\phi + \hat e_1) - d_1\phi_1P(\boldsymbol\phi) + \sum_{k\geq2}\bigl[b_{k-1}(\phi_{k-1} + 1)P(\boldsymbol\phi + \hat e_{k-1} - \hat e_k) - d_k\phi_kP(\boldsymbol\phi)\bigr]\] \[\qquad + \sum_{k\geq1}\bigl[d_{k+1}(\phi_{k+1} + 1)P(\boldsymbol\phi + \hat e_{k+1} - \hat e_k) - b_k\phi_kP(\boldsymbol\phi)\bigr] - b_0P(\boldsymbol\phi).\] Detailed balance for each move, together with the ansatz of independent occupation numbers, \(P_{\text{st}}(\boldsymbol\phi) = \prod_kP_k(\phi_k)/Z\), gives \[P_k(\phi_k) \propto \frac{1}{\phi_k!}\Bigl(\frac{b_0}{d_1}\prod_{i=2}^{k}\frac{b_{i-1}}{d_i}\Bigr)^{\phi_k}.\] For linear rates \(b_i = bi\), \(d_i = di\), with \(x = b/d\) and \(\gamma = b_0/d\), \[P_k(\phi_k) = \frac{1}{\phi_k!}\Bigl(\gamma\frac{x^k}k\Bigr)^{\phi_k}e^{-\gamma x^k/k}:\] each \(\phi_k\) is an independent Poisson variable with mean \(\langle\phi_k\rangle = \gamma x^k/k\), which is again the log-series. The normalisation is \(Z = \exp\bigl(\gamma\sum_kx^k/k\bigr) = (1 - x)^{-\gamma}\).
The total number of species \(S = \sum_k\phi_k\) is a sum of independent Poisson variables, hence Poisson: \[P(S) = \frac{\langle S\rangle^S}{S!}e^{-\langle S\rangle}, \qquad \langle S\rangle = -\gamma\ln(1 - x).\]

4.3.1 Relations between patterns
The grand-canonical picture suggests a coarse-grained view of a community. Species appear at random times, at a rate \(\lambda\) (speciation or immigration), and each persists for a time \(\tau\) drawn from the SPT distribution, independently of the others: an “\(M/G/\infty\) queue”. Then:

the number of species present is Poisson, with mean given by Little’s law: \(\langle S\rangle = \lambda\langle\tau\rangle\);
the SPT and the species richness are linked. With \(p(\tau) \propto \tau^{-2}\) cut off at \(\tau_c = 1/\delta\), \(\langle\tau\rangle \propto \ln\tau_c\), so \(\langle S\rangle \propto \lambda\ln(1/\delta)\). Compare \(-\gamma\ln(1 - x)\) above, with \(1 - x = \delta/d\);
making appearances also random in space, each species occupying a region that grows with its age, turns the SPT into a range-size distribution and hence into a SAR (Suweis, Rinaldo, Maritan, 2012). Temporal and spatial patterns are two faces of the same birth–death–speciation process.

4.4 Metapopulations
Many species live on patchy habitats: ponds, meadows, islands, forest fragments. Levins (1969) introduced the metapopulation, a “population of populations” in which each local population has a substantial risk of extinction and the species persists only regionally, through recolonisation. Hanski applied and extended the idea (e.g. to the Glanville fritillary butterfly in the Åland islands).

4.4.1 The Hanski model
Let \(P_x(t) \in [0, 1]\) be the probability that patch \(x\) is occupied. Occupied patches go extinct at rate \(v_x\); an empty patch is colonised from occupied patches \(y\) at rate \(K_{xy}\): \[\dot P_x = -v_xP_x + (1 - P_x)\sum_yK_{xy}P_y, \qquad K_{xy} = c\,e^{-|x - y|/\xi}\ (y \neq x),\] with \(\xi\) the dispersal distance and \(c\) a colonisation rate (which can include patch sizes). The dynamics keeps \(0 \leq P_x \leq 1\).


4.4.2 Persistence as an eigenvalue problem
The empty state \(P = 0\) is always an equilibrium. Linearising, \(\dot P_x \simeq \sum_y\bigl(K_{xy} - v_x\delta_{xy}\bigr)P_y\). With equal extinction rates \(v_x = v\), the empty state is unstable, and the species persists, if and only if \[\lambda_M > v,\] where \(\lambda_M\) is the largest eigenvalue of the colonisation matrix \(K\), the metapopulation capacity of the landscape. Since \(K\) has positive entries (and is irreducible if every patch can be reached), the Perron–Frobenius theorem guarantees that \(\lambda_M\) is real, simple and dominant, with an eigenvector of positive entries. The landscape’s ability to support the species is summarised in a single number. With heterogeneous \(v_x\), the criterion becomes that the leading eigenvalue of \(E^{-1}K\), with \(E = \operatorname{diag}(v_x)\), exceeds \(1\). Data on the fraction of occupied patches against \(\log\lambda_M\) across patch networks show the predicted threshold.


4.4.3 Translation-invariant landscapes
On a regular lattice with \(v_x = v\) and \(K_{xy} = \hat K_{x-y}\), Fourier modes \(\hat P(q) = \sum_xe^{iqx}P_x\) decouple at linear order: \[\dot{\hat P}(q) = \bigl(-v + \hat K(q)\bigr)\hat P(q), \qquad \hat K(q) = \sum_xe^{iqx}\hat K_x .\] Since \(|\hat K(q)| \leq \hat K(0) = \sum_x\hat K_x\), the most unstable mode is uniform. The species survives iff \(\hat K(0) > v\), and the homogeneous non-trivial equilibrium is \[P^* = 1 - \frac{v}{\hat K(0)} .\] This is a mean-field transcritical bifurcation, the same structure as the SIS epidemic threshold (Chapter 2) and the contact process.


4.4.4 Heterogeneous extinction rates and localisation
Let \(\hat K(0) = 1\) and let the \(v_x\) be drawn independently from a distribution \(Q(v)\). In mean field each patch feels the average occupancy \(m = \frac1N\sum_yP_y\): \[\dot P_x = -v_xP_x + (1 - P_x)m \;\Longrightarrow\; P^*_x = \frac{m^*}{v_x + m^*},\] with self-consistency \(m^* = \int dv\,Q(v)\,\frac{m^*}{v + m^*}\). Besides \(m^* = 0\), a positive solution exists iff \(\int dv\,Q(v)/v > 1\). As the transition is approached, \(m^* \to 0\) and patches with small \(v_x\) dominate the occupancy. How localised the occupancy becomes is measured by the participation ratio \[I = \frac{\langle P^2\rangle}{\langle P\rangle^2}, \qquad \langle P^\ell\rangle = \int dv\,Q(v)\Bigl(\frac{m^*}{v + m^*}\Bigr)^\ell .\] If \(Q\) is bounded away from zero (e.g. uniform on \([\bar v - \Delta, \bar v + \Delta]\)), \(I\) stays finite as \(m^* \to 0\): the species is spread over the landscape. If \(Q(v) \propto v^{\delta - 1}\) near \(v = 0\) (e.g. a Gamma distribution with shape \(\delta < 1\)), then \(\langle P\rangle \propto m^{*\delta}\) and \(\langle P^2\rangle \propto m^{*\delta}\), so \(I \propto m^{*-\delta} \to \infty\). Near extinction the species survives only in a vanishing fraction of exceptionally good patches: localisation. Conservation must then target these refugia.
