title: 13  Whole-brain models and brain criticality
text:
13.3 Whole-brain models

13.3.1 From structure to function
Structural connectivity (SC): DTI tractography gives a weighted network \(W_{ij}\) between \(N\) cortical regions, its weights proportional to the number of fibres. Functional connectivity (FC): the Pearson correlation matrix of resting-state BOLD signals, \[F_{ij} = \frac{\langle x_ix_j\rangle - \langle x_i\rangle\langle x_j\rangle}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}.\] FC is organised into resting-state networks (default mode, visual, sensorimotor, attention…) that are reproducible across subjects. Whole-brain models put a dynamical system on each node, couple the nodes through the connectome, and compare simulated with empirical FC. “Make everything as simple as possible, but not simpler”: the HTC model uses the simplest possible node dynamics.


13.3.2 The HTC model
Each node \(i\) is in one of three states: quiescent \(Q\), excited \(E\) (written \(s_i = 1\)), or refractory \(R\) (\(s_i = 0\) for \(Q\) and \(R\)). Time is discrete and updates are synchronous, following a stochastic Greenberg–Hastings excitable automaton: \[Q \to E \;\text{ if } \sum_jW_{ij}s_j > T, \text{ or spontaneously with probability } r_1; \qquad E \to R \;\text{ with probability } 1; \qquad R \to Q \;\text{ with probability } r_2 .\] A node fires if enough of its neighbours fire (weighted by the connectome) or spontaneously. It then becomes refractory and recovers after a geometric time with mean \(1/r_2\). The threshold \(T\) is the control parameter. Typical values are \(r_1 = 2/N\) (rare spontaneous activation) and \(r_2 = r_1^{1/5}\).
Observables: the mean activity \(\langle A\rangle\), with \(A(t) = \frac1N\sum_is_i(t)\), its standard deviation \(\sigma(A)\), and the average sizes of the largest and second-largest clusters \(\langle S_1\rangle\), \(\langle S_2\rangle\). Clusters are sets of structurally connected nodes that are simultaneously active.


13.3.3 Two phases and a transition

Small \(T\) (supercritical): even weak connections propagate activity. Activity is high and sustained, fluctuations are fast and uncorrelated, and one giant cluster dominates.
Large \(T\) (subcritical): only the strongest connections transmit. Activity is low and sparse, made of short-lived local events.
Intermediate \(T_c\): a continuous transition. \(\langle S_1\rangle\) drops, \(\sigma(A)\) peaks and \(\langle S_2\rangle\) peaks, the signature of a percolation-like transition, used to locate \(T_c\). At \(T_c\) the cluster-size distribution is a truncated power law, \(P(S) \sim S^{-\alpha}\) with \(\alpha \simeq 3/2\).

Comparing with data: the Pearson correlation between simulated and empirical FC, \(\rho(F_m, F_e)\), and the similarity of simulated resting-state networks to empirical templates are both maximal near \(T_c\). A model of the healthy brain matches its spontaneous activity best at criticality.


13.3.4 Homeostatic plasticity
In the raw model, activity is dominated by hubs, nodes with large total input strength \(W_i = \sum_jW_{ij}\). Rocha et al. (2018) proposed a homeostatic normalisation that equalises the input of every region, \[\widetilde W_{ij} = \frac{W_{ij}}{\sum_jW_{ij}},\] so every node has unit in-strength, as if synapses had adjusted to keep each region’s excitability constant. With \(\widetilde W\):

the transition becomes sharper and the \(\langle S_2\rangle\) peak more pronounced;
the cluster-size power law extends about three times further (cut-off \(\sim 15\) instead of \(\sim 5\)) with \(\alpha = 3/2\) (against \(\alpha \simeq 1.75\) without normalisation);
the match with empirical FC improves by a factor of about \(1.5\) at the group level and up to \(2\) for individuals.



13.3.5 Personalised models
Using the structural and functional matrices of \(43\) healthy subjects (\(N = 264\) regions, Rudie et al., 2012), each individual connectome can be simulated. Without normalisation each subject has a different critical threshold, but the ratio \(T_c/\langle W\rangle \simeq 0.16\) is nearly constant, as predicted by mean field (\(T_c\) scales with the mean weight). With normalisation all subjects collapse onto the same curves with \(T_c \simeq 0.15\): homeostasis makes the critical point universal across individuals. This makes personalised modelling feasible.


13.3.6 Stroke and recovery
Applied to stroke patients (Corbetta et al., 2015), personalised models show that lesions push the brain away from criticality. Activity and cluster statistics of patients deviate from those of controls, with a weaker transition (lower \(\sigma(A)\) and \(\langle S_2\rangle\) peaks). During recovery, from 3 months to 1 year after the stroke, patients move back toward critical behaviour. The changes in these criticality measures correlate with the recovery of behavioural scores across subjects (Rocha et al., 2022). Criticality is a candidate biomarker of healthy brain dynamics.

section: 13.4 Mean-field theory of the HTC model
text:
13.4 Mean-field theory of the HTC model

13.4.1 Master equation
Consider the fully connected, normalised case, \(\widetilde W_{ij} = 1/N\). The input to a node is the fraction of active nodes, \(\sum_j\widetilde W_{ij}s_j - T = x - T\). Let \(n_x\), \(n_y\) be the numbers of excited and refractory nodes (\(n_Q = N - n_x - n_y\)). In continuous time the transitions are \[(n_x, n_y) \to (n_x + 1, n_y) \;\text{at rate } (N - n_x - n_y)\,r_{\text{act}}, \qquad r_{\text{act}} = r_1 + (1 - r_1)\Theta(x - T),\] \[(n_x, n_y) \to (n_x - 1, n_y + 1) \;\text{at rate } n_x, \qquad (n_x, n_y) \to (n_x, n_y - 1) \;\text{at rate } r_2n_y .\] With densities \(x = n_x/N\), \(y = n_y/N\), the Kramers–Moyal expansion (Chapters 2 and 5) gives a Fokker–Planck equation with drift and diffusion \[A_1 = (1 - x - y)r_{\text{act}} - x, \qquad A_2 = x - r_2y,\] \[B_{11} = (1 - x - y)r_{\text{act}} + x, \qquad B_{22} = r_2y + x, \qquad B_{12} = B_{21} = -x,\] the off-diagonal term coming from the \(E \to R\) reaction, which moves one unit from \(x\) to \(y\).


13.4.2 Equilibria in the thermodynamic limit
For \(N \to \infty\), \(\dot x = A_1\), \(\dot y = A_2\). Two regimes arise from the step function.

Supercritical branch (\(x > T\), \(r_{\text{act}} = 1\)): \(y_+ = \frac{1}{2r_2 + 1}\), \(x_+ = r_2y_+\). It exists iff \(x_+ > T\), i.e. \(T < T_+ \equiv \frac{r_2}{2r_2 + 1}\). The activity is independent of \(r_1\): it is self-sustained by interactions.
Subcritical branch (\(x \leq T\), \(r_{\text{act}} = r_1\)): \(y_- = \frac{r_1}{r_2 + (r_2 + 1)r_1}\), \(x_- = r_2y_-\). It exists iff \(T \geq T_- \equiv x_-\).

Since \(r_1 < 1\), \(T_- < T_+\). Three regions follow: for \(T < T_-\) only the active phase exists, for \(T > T_+\) only the quiescent phase, and for \(T_- < T < T_+\) both are stable, each with its own basin of attraction. In mean field the transition is therefore discontinuous (first order), with hysteresis: increasing \(T\) the system jumps down at \(T_+\), decreasing it jumps up at \(T_-\). On real, sparse and heterogeneous connectomes the transition is smoothed into the continuous-looking transition seen in simulations.


13.4.3 Stability
At the supercritical point, \[J_+ = \begin{pmatrix}-2 & -1\\ 1 & -r_2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda_+ = \frac{-(2 + r_2) \pm\sqrt{r_2^2 - 4r_2}}{2}:\] always stable, a focus for \(r_2 < 4\) and a node for \(r_2 > 4\). At the subcritical point, \[J_- = \begin{pmatrix}-1 - r_1 & -r_1\\ 1 & -r_2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda_- = \frac{-(1 + r_1 + r_2) \pm\sqrt{(1 + r_1 + r_2)^2 - 4(r_1 + r_2 + r_1r_2)}}{2}:\] always stable, and a focus iff \(r_1 - 2\sqrt{r_1} + 1 < r_2 < r_1 + 2\sqrt{r_1} + 1\).


13.4.4 Fluctuations and oscillations
Around a stable equilibrium the linear noise approximation gives \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta} = J\boldsymbol\zeta + \boldsymbol\eta\), with \(\langle\boldsymbol\eta\boldsymbol\eta^\top\rangle = B\) evaluated at the fixed point, and the power spectrum \[P_x(\omega) = \frac{\alpha + \beta\omega^2}{(\omega^2 - \Omega_0^2)^2 + \Gamma^2\omega^2}, \qquad \alpha = B_{11}J_{22}^2 - 2B_{12}J_{12}J_{22} + B_{22}J_{12}^2, \quad \beta = B_{11}, \quad \Omega_0^2 = \det J, \quad \Gamma = -\operatorname{tr}J,\] the formula of Chapter 5. In the fully connected model the foci are strongly damped (\(\operatorname{Re}\lambda \simeq -1\)) and spectral peaks are weak. Network structure changes this: on connectomes and random graphs, near the critical threshold the model shows collective oscillations and a peak in the power spectrum. Activity propagates as waves on Erdős–Rényi graphs and as localised patterns on the connectome. Criticality and structure jointly drive emergent oscillations (Barzon et al., 2022).

13.5 Exercises

(Branching ratio) In a branching process each active neuron activates each of \(K = 10\) downstream neurons independently with probability \(p\). (a) What is the branching ratio? (b) For which \(p\) is the process critical? (c) For \(p = 0.08\), what is the mean avalanche size?


Solution. 

\(\sigma = Kp\). (b) \(p_c = 1/K = 0.1\). (c) For \(\sigma < 1\) the mean total size is \(\sum_t\sigma^t = 1/(1 - \sigma) = 1/(1 - 0.8) = 5\) neurons. It diverges as \(\sigma \to 1\) with exponent \(1\), the susceptibility of this mean-field transition.



(Critical avalanche sizes) For binary branching (each active unit has \(0\) or \(2\) offspring with probability \(1/2\)), solve \(Q(z) = z\,g(Q(z))\) exactly and verify \(P(s) \sim s^{-3/2}\).


Solution. \(g(z) = \frac12(1 + z^2)\), so \(Q = \frac z2(1 + Q^2)\), i.e. \(zQ^2 - 2Q + z = 0\) and \(Q(z) = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - z^2}}{z}\), taking the root regular at \(z = 0\). Expanding \(\sqrt{1 - z^2} = 1 - \sum_{k\geq1}\frac{(2k - 3)!!}{2^kk!}z^{2k}\) gives non-zero probabilities only for odd sizes, \(P(s = 2k - 1) = \frac{(2k - 3)!!}{2^kk!}\). By Stirling \((2k - 3)!!/(2^kk!) \sim \frac{1}{2\sqrt\pi}k^{-3/2}\), so \(P(s) \sim s^{-3/2}\). The square-root singularity of \(Q\) at \(z = 1\) is the generating-function signature of the exponent \(3/2\).


(HTC mean field) For \(r_1 = r_2 = 0.1\), compute \(x_\pm\), \(T_\pm\) and the nature of both equilibria. What happens to the activity if \(T\) is slowly increased from \(0\) to \(0.1\) and then decreased back?


Solution. \(y_+ = 1/1.2 = 0.833\), \(x_+ = 0.0833 = T_+\); \(y_- = 0.1/(0.1 + 0.11) = 0.476\), \(x_- = 0.0476 = T_-\). \(J_+\) has eigenvalues \(-1.05 \pm 0.31i\) (stable focus); \(J_-\) has \(-0.99\) and \(-0.21\) (stable node, since \(r_2 = 0.1\) is outside \((1 - 2\sqrt{0.1} + 0.1,\ 1 + 2\sqrt{0.1} + 0.1) = (0.47, 1.73)\)). Increasing \(T\) from \(0\), the system stays on the active branch (\(x \simeq 0.083\)) until \(T_+ = 0.083\), then drops to \(x_- \simeq 0.048\). Decreasing \(T\), it stays low until \(T_- = 0.048\) and then jumps back up. The hysteresis loop spans \([0.048, 0.083]\), the region of bistability.


(Homeostatic normalisation) Why does the normalisation \(\widetilde W_{ij} = W_{ij}/\sum_jW_{ij}\) make the critical threshold the same for all subjects in mean field, and what does it change for hubs?


Solution. After normalisation every node’s total input weight is \(1\), so a node’s input is a weighted average of its neighbours’ states, bounded by \(1\), whatever the subject’s overall fibre density. In mean field the activation condition is \(x > T\) for every node and every subject, hence a universal \(T_c\). Without normalisation the input of node \(i\) is \(\sim W_ix\), so \(T_c \propto \langle W\rangle\), which differs between subjects (hence the constant ratio \(T_c/\langle W\rangle\)). For hubs, normalisation reduces their dominance: before it, high-strength nodes are almost always active and enslave the dynamics; after it, every region contributes similarly, which enriches the repertoire of patterns and improves agreement with functional data.


(Diffusion matrix of the HTC model) Derive \(B\) from the three reactions and evaluate it at the supercritical equilibrium for \(r_2 = 0.1\).


Solution. Reactions with state changes and rates per \(N\): activation \((+1, 0)\) at \((1 - x - y)r_{\text{act}}\); excited to refractory \((-1, +1)\) at \(x\); recovery \((0, -1)\) at \(r_2y\). Then \(B = \sum_j\mathbf v_j\mathbf v_j^\top a_j\): \(B_{11} = (1 - x - y)r_{\text{act}} + x\), \(B_{22} = x + r_2y\), \(B_{12} = -x\). At \(x_+ = 0.083\), \(y_+ = 0.833\), \(r_{\text{act}} = 1\): \(B_{11} = 0.083 + 0.083 = 0.167\), \(B_{22} = 0.083 + 0.083 = 0.167\), \(B_{12} = -0.083\). The negative correlation reflects that each \(E \to R\) event lowers \(x\) and raises \(y\) together.

title: 14  The cell and stochastic gene expression
text:
14.1 The cell and the central dogma
The third module moves inside the cell. Genes are the units, proteins and mRNA are the “populations”, and transcription factors play the role of interactions. Molecule numbers are small (a few to a few thousand copies per cell), so noise is not a correction but a defining feature: genetically identical cells in identical environments express genes at very different levels. This chapter introduces the molecular machinery of gene expression and solves the two classic stochastic models: the one-stage (birth–death) model, which gives Poisson statistics, and the two-stage (mRNA–protein) model, which gives protein bursts and a negative binomial distribution, directly comparable with single-cell data.
A cell is a crowded, compartmentalised reactor. Its genome (about \(4.6\) Mb in E. coli, \(3\) Gb in humans) encodes genes that are transcribed by RNA polymerase into messenger RNA (mRNA), which is translated by ribosomes into proteins. Each codon of three nucleotides (\(4^3 = 64\) possibilities) codes for one of \(20\) amino acids, plus stop signals. A protein is a chain of \(50\)–\(1000\) amino acids that folds into a specific three-dimensional structure (Chapter 18). The folding is driven by the free energy \(F = E - TS\): hydrophobic residues hide in the core, and the folded state has low energy but also low entropy.
Transcription factors (TFs) are proteins that bind specific DNA sequences (operators) near a gene’s promoter and activate or repress its transcription. Gene expression is therefore regulated by the products of other genes, forming gene regulatory networks (Chapters 16–17).
Typical numbers for E. coli show why noise matters:

title: 14  The cell and stochastic gene expression
text:
14.2 The one-stage model
Ignore mRNA and let a protein be produced at rate \(v\) and degraded (or diluted) at rate \(d\) per molecule: \[\varnothing \xrightarrow{v} P, \qquad P \xrightarrow{d} \varnothing .\] The master equation for \(P_n(t)\), the probability of \(n\) proteins, is the birth–death equation of Chapter 2 with constant birth rate: \[\frac{dP_n}{dt} = v(P_{n-1} - P_n) + d\bigl[(n + 1)P_{n+1} - nP_n\bigr].\] With the generating function \(G(z, t) = \sum_nP_nz^n\), using \(\sum_nnP_nz^n = z\partial_zG\), \[\partial_tG = (z - 1)\bigl(vG - d\,\partial_zG\bigr).\] At stationarity \(\partial_zG = \frac vdG\), so \(G = e^{(v/d)(z - 1)}\): a Poisson distribution with mean \(\langle n\rangle = v/d\) and Fano factor \(\sigma^2/\langle n\rangle = 1\). The time-dependent solution from \(n = 0\) is Poisson with mean \(\frac vd(1 - e^{-dt})\), and relaxation happens on the time scale \(1/d\).
A single molecule survives a time \(t\) with probability \(P_>(t) = e^{-dt}\), so its half-life is \(t_{1/2} = \ln2/d\): minutes for mRNA, while stable proteins are mostly removed by dilution at cell division.

14  The cell and stochastic gene expression

title: 14  The cell and stochastic gene expression
text:
14.3 The two-stage model
Experiments find Fano factors much larger than one. The reason is that proteins are made from a small number of mRNAs, each producing many proteins. The two-stage model includes both species: \[\text{DNA} \xrightarrow{v_0} \text{mRNA}, \qquad \text{mRNA} \xrightarrow{d_0} \varnothing, \qquad \text{mRNA} \xrightarrow{v_1} \text{mRNA} + P, \qquad P \xrightarrow{d_1} \varnothing .\] With \(m\) mRNAs and \(n\) proteins, \[\frac{dP_{m,n}}{dt} = v_0(P_{m-1,n} - P_{m,n}) + v_1m(P_{m,n-1} - P_{m,n}) + d_0\bigl[(m + 1)P_{m+1,n} - mP_{m,n}\bigr] + d_1\bigl[(n + 1)P_{m,n+1} - nP_{m,n}\bigr].\] The generating function \(F(z', z, t) = \sum_{m,n}P_{m,n}z'^mz^n\) obeys, with \(u = z' - 1\) and \(v = z - 1\), \[\partial_tF = v_0u\,F + v_1(1 + u)v\,\partial_uF - d_0u\,\partial_uF - d_1v\,\partial_vF .\]

14.3.1 Moments
From the equations for the means and second moments (or by differentiating \(F\) at \(u = v = 0\)), \[\langle m\rangle = \frac{v_0}{d_0}, \qquad \langle n\rangle = \frac{v_0v_1}{d_0d_1}, \qquad \frac{\sigma_n^2}{\langle n\rangle} = 1 + \frac{v_1}{d_0 + d_1}.\] Define the burst frequency \(a = v_0/d_1\) (mRNAs made per protein lifetime) and the burst size \(b = v_1/d_0\) (proteins made per mRNA). Then \(\langle n\rangle = ab\), and when \(\gamma = d_0/d_1 \gg 1\) (mRNA much shorter-lived than protein), the Fano factor is \(1 + b\). Protein noise is set by the burst size, not by the mean.


14.3.2 Bursts and the negative binomial
When \(\gamma \gg 1\), each mRNA lives briefly and produces a geometrically distributed burst of proteins with mean \(b\) (each step, translation with probability \(\frac{v_1}{v_1 + d_0}\) or decay). Bursts arrive as a Poisson process at rate \(v_0\), and proteins decay slowly. Solving the PDE by characteristics in this limit (Shahrezaei and Swain, 2008), the mRNA variable relaxes adiabatically to \(u \simeq \frac{bv}{1 - bv}\), and the stationary protein generating function becomes \[F(z) = \Bigl(\frac{1}{1 + b - bz}\Bigr)^a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_n = \frac{\Gamma(a + n)}{\Gamma(n + 1)\Gamma(a)}\Bigl(\frac{b}{1 + b}\Bigr)^n\Bigl(\frac{1}{1 + b}\Bigr)^a :\] a negative binomial with mean \(ab\) and variance \(ab(1 + b)\). The same distribution appeared for species abundances (Chapter 3): there, too, it reflected multiplicative “bursty” growth with immigration. The continuum limit is a Gamma distribution with shape \(a\) and scale \(b\).

Two genes with the same mean of \(50\) proteins:

\(a = 20\), \(b = 2.5\): frequent small bursts. The distribution is nearly Gaussian, with Fano factor \(3.5\) (Gillespie simulation: \(3.4\)).
\(a = 0.5\), \(b = 100\): rare large bursts. The distribution is strongly skewed, with a peak at zero and a long tail, and the Fano factor is \(101\) (simulation: \(102\)).

Time traces of the second gene show long silent periods interrupted by sudden jumps, exactly what is seen in single-molecule experiments (Cai, Friedman and Xie, 2006).



14.3.3 Intrinsic and extrinsic noise
Elowitz et al. (2002) put two copies of the same promoter, driving different fluorescent proteins, into the same E. coli cell. Fluctuations that affect both copies equally (cell size, ribosome and polymerase numbers, cell-cycle phase) are extrinsic. Fluctuations that make the two copies differ (the randomness of individual reaction events) are intrinsic. With normalised expressions \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \[\eta_{\text{int}}^2 = \frac{\langle(x_1 - x_2)^2\rangle}{2\langle x_1\rangle\langle x_2\rangle}, \qquad \eta_{\text{ext}}^2 = \frac{\langle x_1x_2\rangle - \langle x_1\rangle\langle x_2\rangle}{\langle x_1\rangle\langle x_2\rangle}.\] Both contributions are comparable in bacteria. The models of this chapter describe intrinsic noise; extrinsic noise enters as slow fluctuations of the rates.

title: 14  The cell and stochastic gene expression
text:
14.4 Why noise matters
Noise is not only a nuisance. Bet hedging: in fluctuating environments, populations in which some cells randomly express a stress-response program survive sudden stresses, as in bacterial persistence to antibiotics. Cell-fate decisions: noise can push cells across thresholds of bistable circuits (Chapter 16), as in the decision of B. subtilis to become competent or of phage λ to choose lysis or lysogeny. Conversely, cells suppress noise where precision matters, with negative feedback (Chapter 16) and with multiple gene copies.

title: 14  The cell and stochastic gene expression
text:
14.5 Exercises

(One-stage model) Show that \(G(z, t) = \exp\bigl[\frac vd(1 - e^{-dt})(z - 1)\bigr]\) solves the one-stage generating-function equation with \(P_n(0) = \delta_{n0}\). What are the mean, variance and half-life?


Solution. With \(\mu(t) = \frac vd(1 - e^{-dt})\), \(G = e^{\mu(z - 1)}\), so \(\partial_tG = \dot\mu(z - 1)G = ve^{-dt}(z - 1)G\) and \(\partial_zG = \mu G\). The right-hand side is \((z - 1)(v - d\mu)G = (z - 1)ve^{-dt}G\), equal to the left. At \(t = 0\), \(G = 1\). The distribution is Poisson at all times, with mean \(=\) variance \(= \mu(t) \to v/d\). One molecule survives with \(e^{-dt}\), so \(t_{1/2} = \ln2/d\).


(Two-stage moments) Derive \(\langle m\rangle\), \(\langle n\rangle\) and the protein Fano factor from the moment equations of the two-stage model.


Solution. Means: \(\dot{\langle m\rangle} = v_0 - d_0\langle m\rangle\) and \(\dot{\langle n\rangle} = v_1\langle m\rangle - d_1\langle n\rangle\), so \(\langle m\rangle = v_0/d_0\) and \(\langle n\rangle = v_0v_1/(d_0d_1)\). Second moments at stationarity (writing covariances): \(\sigma_m^2 = \langle m\rangle\) (Poisson); \(\frac{d}{dt}\mathrm{Cov}(m, n) = v_1\sigma_m^2 - (d_0 + d_1)\mathrm{Cov} = 0\), so \(\mathrm{Cov} = \frac{v_1\langle m\rangle}{d_0 + d_1}\); \(\frac{d}{dt}\sigma_n^2 = v_1\langle m\rangle + d_1\langle n\rangle + 2v_1\mathrm{Cov} - 2d_1\sigma_n^2 = 0\). Using \(v_1\langle m\rangle = d_1\langle n\rangle\): \(\sigma_n^2 = \langle n\rangle + \frac{v_1}{d_1}\mathrm{Cov} = \langle n\rangle\bigl(1 + \frac{v_1}{d_0 + d_1}\bigr)\). Fano factor \(1 + \frac{v_1}{d_0 + d_1} \to 1 + b\) for \(d_0 \gg d_1\).


(Bursts by simulation) Simulate the two-stage model with the Gillespie algorithm for \(d_0 = 1\), \(d_1 = 0.01\) (in min\(^{-1}\)), and \((a, b) = (20, 2.5)\) and \((0.5, 100)\). Compare the time-averaged histograms with the negative binomial.


Solution. Rates: \(v_0 = ad_1\), \(v_1 = bd_0\). Time-weighted statistics over \(3\times10^5\) min give mean \(50.6\) and Fano factor \(3.40\) for \((20, 2.5)\), and mean \(49.7\) and Fano factor \(101.7\) for \((0.5, 100)\), matching \(ab = 50\) and \(1 + b = 3.5\), \(101\). Histograms agree with \(\mathrm{NB}(a, b/(1 + b))\): the first is unimodal around \(50\), the second has its mode at \(0\) and a long tail up to several hundred. With \(a < 1\) the gene is “off” most of the time.


(Negative binomial from bursts) Assume bursts arrive at rate \(v_0\), each adding a geometric number of proteins with mean \(b\), and proteins decay at rate \(d_1\). Show that the stationary generating function is \((1 + b - bz)^{-a}\) with \(a = v_0/d_1\).


Solution. A geometric burst has generating function \(g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + b - bz}\). The master equation in generating-function form is \(\partial_tF = v_0[g(z) - 1]F - d_1(z - 1)\partial_zF\). At stationarity \(\partial_z\ln F = \frac{a[g(z) - 1]}{z - 1} = \frac{ab}{1 + b - bz}\), which integrates to \(\ln F = -a\ln(1 + b - bz)\), using \(F(1) = 1\). Hence \(F = (1 + b - bz)^{-a}\), the negative binomial. Its mean is \(F'(1) = ab\) and its variance \(ab(1 + b)\).


(Intrinsic noise) For the one-stage model, compute \(\eta^2 = \sigma^2/\langle n\rangle^2\). How many proteins are needed for \(10\%\) noise? What if the protein is made in bursts of size \(b = 20\)?


Solution. Poisson: \(\eta^2 = 1/\langle n\rangle\), so \(10\%\) noise (\(\eta^2 = 0.01\)) needs \(\langle n\rangle = 100\). With bursts, \(\eta^2 = (1 + b)/\langle n\rangle\), so \(\langle n\rangle = 2100\) proteins are needed for the same precision: bursting is costly for precision, which is one reason why highly expressed, noise-sensitive genes tend to use high transcription and low translation rates (small \(b\)).

title: 15  Life at the micro-scale: information, ratchets and molecular motors
text:
15.1 Energy scales of the cell
Inside a cell, molecular machines transport cargo, copy DNA and contract muscles, all while being kicked around by thermal fluctuations with energies comparable to their own working energy. Can such machines extract work from noise, apparently violating the second law? This chapter revisits the paradoxes of Maxwell’s demon and Feynman’s ratchet, introduces Landauer’s principle (information is physical), and builds the stochastic models of molecular and Brownian motors. Their consistency with thermodynamics rests on the principle of local detailed balance.
At \(T = 300\) K, the thermal energy is \(k_BT = R T/N_A = 4.1\times10^{-21}\) J \(\simeq 4.1\) pN·nm \(\simeq 0.6\) kcal/mol \(\simeq 25\) meV. Molecular processes involve energies of a few to a few tens of \(k_BT\):

title: 15  Life at the micro-scale: information, ratchets and molecular motors
text:
ATP hydrolysis, \(\text{ATP} \rightleftharpoons \text{ADP} + \text{P}_i\), releases \(\Delta G^0 \simeq -30\) kJ/mol \(\simeq 5\times10^{-20}\) J \(\simeq 12\,k_BT\) under standard conditions, and about \(20\)–\(25\,k_BT\) under cellular conditions, where ATP is far from equilibrium with its products.
A water molecule at \(300\) K moves at \(\sqrt{\langle v^2\rangle} = \sqrt{3RT/M} \simeq 650\) m/s and undergoes a collision every \(\sim 10^{-13}\) s. A protein in water experiences \(\sim 10^{13}\) collisions per second, so its motion is overdamped Brownian motion: inertia is irrelevant (low Reynolds number), and any directed motion must be produced against incessant random forces.

title: 15  Life at the micro-scale: information, ratchets and molecular motors
section: 15.2 Maxwell’s demon and the cost of information
text:
15.2 Maxwell’s demon and the cost of information
Maxwell (1867) imagined a demon controlling a trapdoor between two gas compartments at the same temperature. Letting fast molecules pass only from left to right and slow ones from right to left, it would create a temperature difference, \(T_R > T_L\), without doing work, decreasing the entropy of an isolated system. This contradicts the second law.
Szilard’s engine (1929) makes it quantitative with one molecule in a box at temperature \(T\). Insert a partition in the middle, measure on which side the molecule is (one bit of information), and let it push the partition isothermally to the far wall. The extracted work is \[W = \int_{V/2}^Vp\,dV = k_BT\ln2,\] seemingly from a single heat bath.
The resolution came from the physics of computation. Bennett (1982) showed that measurement can be done without dissipation, but the demon’s memory must eventually be reset to be reused, and:

Erasing one bit of information in an environment at temperature \(T\) dissipates at least \[Q \geq k_BT\ln2,\] i.e. it increases the entropy of the environment by at least \(\Delta S \geq k_B\ln2\).

Including the memory, the total entropy balance \(\Delta S_{\text{gas}} + \Delta S_{\text{memory}} + \Delta S_{\text{environment}} \geq 0\) is respected: the work extracted by the Szilard engine is paid for by erasing the measurement record. Information is physical. Landauer’s bound was verified experimentally with a colloidal particle in a double-well optical trap (Bérut et al., 2012): erasing the bit (forcing the particle into one well, whatever the initial well) dissipates on average \(k_BT\ln2\) in the slow limit. Conversely, an information engine can convert information into work at most \(k_BT\ln2\) per bit.

title: 15  Life at the micro-scale: information, ratchets and molecular motors
text:
15.3 Feynman’s ratchet and pawl
Feynman (1962) analysed a microscopic ratchet: a paddle wheel immersed in a gas at temperature \(T_2\) is connected by an axle to a ratchet with a spring-loaded pawl at temperature \(T_1\). The pawl lets the ratchet rotate only one way, so it seems that random collisions with the paddles would rotate the axle and lift a weight.
They do not when \(T_1 = T_2\). The pawl itself is thermally agitated: with the same probability \(\propto e^{-\epsilon/k_BT}\) with which a collision supplies the energy \(\epsilon\) to advance one tooth, the pawl is thermally lifted and the ratchet slips back. Forward and backward rates balance, and no net motion occurs. If \(T_2 > T_1\), the device works as a heat engine, with efficiency bounded by Carnot’s, \(\eta \leq 1 - T_1/T_2\). (Feynman’s original claim that it reaches the Carnot efficiency is incorrect: heat conduction through the axle makes it irreversible; Parrondo and Español, 1996.) Rectifying equilibrium fluctuations is impossible; directed motion needs a source of free energy that drives the system out of equilibrium.

title: 15  Life at the micro-scale: information, ratchets and molecular motors
text:
15.4 Brownian motors

15.4.1 Equilibrium in a periodic potential
Consider an overdamped particle in a periodic, asymmetric (“sawtooth”) potential \(V(x + L) = V(x)\). At equilibrium its density is the Boltzmann distribution \(P_{\text{eq}}(x) \propto e^{-\beta V(x)}\). On an infinite line the normalisation diverges, but the reduced density \[\hat P(x) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}P(x + nL), \qquad \hat P_{\text{eq}}(x) = \frac{e^{-\beta V(x)}}{\hat Z}, \qquad \hat Z = \int_0^Le^{-\beta V(x)}dx,\] is well defined on one period. Being an equilibrium state, it carries zero current, \(J = 0\): asymmetry of the potential alone does not produce motion. With an external force \(F\), the tilted potential \(V(x) - Fx\) produces a drift in the direction of the force, whatever the asymmetry.


15.4.2 Rectifying noise out of equilibrium
Directed motion appears when the potential is switched or tilted in time, which requires an energy input. In a flashing ratchet the sawtooth is periodically turned on and off. While off, the particle diffuses symmetrically. When the potential is switched on again, the particle is captured in the well toward which it has a shorter distance to the nearest maximum. Because of the asymmetry, more particles cross the short side than the long side, and a net current flows, even against a small load. A rocking ratchet (a periodic, zero-mean tilt) or temperature oscillations work the same way. Brownian motors are theoretical and artificial devices (optical ratchets, colloids, electrons in asymmetric structures) that turn unbiased fluctuations into directed motion with the help of a non-equilibrium driving.

title: 15  Life at the micro-scale: information, ratchets and molecular motors
text:
15.5 Molecular motors

15.5.1 Biological motors
Cells contain three families of molecular motors, proteins that convert the chemical free energy of ATP into mechanical work:

kinesins walk along microtubules toward their plus end, carrying vesicles in axons, in \(8\) nm steps, one ATP per step, at about \(1\,\mu\)m/s;
dyneins walk toward the minus end of microtubules (retrograde transport, cilia and flagella);
myosins move on actin filaments (muscle contraction, transport).

Compared with Brownian motors, they are tightly coupled to chemistry: each step is associated with a conformational change triggered by binding and hydrolysis of ATP. Directionality comes from the asymmetric structure of the track and of the motor, and their motion is nearly deterministic at high ATP concentration.


15.5.2 A two-state model
The simplest model has the motor on a periodic track with sites \(x = na\) and two internal states, \(1\) and \(2\) (e.g. ATP-free and ATP-bound). The transitions are:

chemical: \(1 \to 2\) by ATP binding/hydrolysis, at rate \(K_+\); backward at rate \(K_-\), both at the same site;
mechanical: from state \(2\) at site \(n\) to state \(1\) at site \(n + 1\) at rate \(W_+\), and backward at rate \(W_-\).

For the site-summed probabilities \(P_i(t) = \sum_nP_i(n, t)\), \[\dot P_1 = (K_- + W_+)P_2 - (K_+ + W_-)P_1, \qquad P_1 + P_2 = 1,\] so at stationarity \[P_2^* = \frac{K_+ + W_-}{K_+ + K_- + W_+ + W_-}.\] The mean velocity is \(a\) times the net rate of forward mechanical steps: \[v = a\bigl(W_+P_2^* - W_-P_1^*\bigr) = a\,\frac{W_+K_+ - W_-K_-}{K_+ + K_- + W_+ + W_-}.\] The motor moves forward iff \(W_+K_+ > W_-K_-\): the product of the forward rates around a cycle must exceed that of the backward rates. In equilibrium the two products are equal (Kolmogorov’s criterion for detailed balance), and \(v = 0\).


15.5.3 Local detailed balance and thermodynamic consistency
How are the rates constrained by thermodynamics? For a transition \(x' \to x\) that exchanges heat with a bath, local detailed balance requires \[\frac{W_{x'\to x}}{W_{x\to x'}} = e^{Q_{\text{bath}}/k_BT} = e^{\Delta S_{\text{bath}}/k_B},\] where \(Q_{\text{bath}}\) is the heat released to the environment. By the first law, \(\Delta E = Q + W + \sum_i\mu_i\Delta N_i\), where \(W\) is mechanical work done on the system and the last term is the chemical work. Over a full cycle the motor returns to the same internal state, advances by \(a\) against a load \(F\) (work \(-Fa\)), and converts one ATP into ADP and \(\text{P}_i\), with \(\Delta\mu = \mu_{\text{ATP}} - \mu_{\text{ADP}} - \mu_{\text{P}_i}\). Hence \[\frac{W_+K_+}{W_-K_-} = e^{\beta(\Delta\mu - Fa)}.\]

With \(\Delta\mu = 0\) and \(F = 0\) (equilibrium), forward and backward cycles are equally likely, and \(v = 0\).
The motor moves forward iff \(\Delta\mu > Fa\). The stall force is \(F_s = \Delta\mu/a\); beyond it the motor walks backward, and at high enough force it can even synthesise ATP. For kinesin (\(a = 8\) nm, \(\Delta\mu \simeq 20\)–\(25\,k_BT\)) this gives \(F_s \simeq 10\)–\(13\) pN, while measured stall forces are \(6\)–\(7\) pN: kinesin works at an efficiency of about \(50\%\).
The entropy production per cycle is \(\beta(\Delta\mu - Fa) \geq 0\), and the thermodynamic efficiency \(\eta = Fa/\Delta\mu \leq 1\), with equality only at stall, where the speed vanishes.

These are instances of stochastic thermodynamics, which extends the first and second laws to single trajectories of small systems. One of its results is that the ratio of the probabilities of a trajectory and its time reverse equals \(e^{\Delta S_{\text{tot}}/k_B}\) (fluctuation theorems).

title: 15  Life at the micro-scale: information, ratchets and molecular motors
text:
15.6 Exercises

(Szilard engine) Compute the work extracted by isothermal expansion of a one-molecule gas from \(V/2\) to \(V\), and the minimal heat dissipated by resetting the memory. Express both at \(300\) K in joules and in units of the ATP free energy.


Solution. \(W = \int_{V/2}^V\frac{k_BT}{V'}dV' = k_BT\ln2 = 2.9\times10^{-21}\) J at \(300\) K. Resetting costs \(Q \geq k_BT\ln2\), the same amount, so the cycle produces no net work, as the second law requires. ATP releases about \(5\times10^{-20}\) J (\(12\,k_BT\), standard conditions), so one ATP could pay for erasing about \(17\) bits at the Landauer limit. Real cellular information processing (e.g. sensing by receptors) dissipates many times more per bit.


(No current at equilibrium) For an overdamped particle in a periodic potential, the Fokker–Planck current is \(J = -D\bigl(\partial_xP + \beta V'(x)P\bigr)\). Show that the stationary periodic solution has \(J = 0\) when \(V(x + L) = V(x)\), and compute \(J\) for a tilted potential \(V(x) - Fx\) to first order in \(F\).


Solution. At stationarity \(J\) is constant. Write \(J = -De^{-\beta V}\partial_x(e^{\beta V}P)\), so \(\partial_x(e^{\beta V}P) = -\frac JDe^{\beta V}\). Integrating over a period with \(P\) and \(V\) periodic, the left side integrates to zero, while the right side integrates to \(-\frac JD\int_0^Le^{\beta V}dx \neq 0\). Hence \(J = 0\) and \(P \propto e^{-\beta V}\). With a tilt, \(e^{\beta(V - Fx)}P\) increases by the factor \(e^{-\beta FL}\) over a period, and to first order in \(F\) the particle drifts with velocity \(v = \beta D_{\text{eff}}F\), where \(D_{\text{eff}} = \frac{DL^2}{\int_0^Le^{\beta V}dx\int_0^Le^{-\beta V}dx} \leq D\) (the Lifson–Jackson formula). The drift is along the force, with a mobility reduced by the potential barriers, whatever the asymmetry of \(V\).


(Two-state motor) For \(K_+ = 100\), \(K_- = 1\), \(W_+ = 200\), \(W_- = 2\) (in s\(^{-1}\)) and \(a = 8\) nm, compute \(P_2^*\), the velocity, and the free energy per cycle \(k_BT\ln\frac{W_+K_+}{W_-K_-}\). What load stalls the motor?


Solution. Sum of rates \(= 303\) s\(^{-1}\). \(P_2^* = (100 + 2)/303 = 0.337\). \(v = 8\,\text{nm}\times\frac{200\times100 - 2\times1}{303} = 8\times66.0 = 528\) nm/s. Cycle affinity \(\ln(20000/2) = \ln10^4 = 9.2\), so \(\Delta\mu - Fa = 9.2\,k_BT\) at zero load. The stall force is \(F_s = 9.2\,k_BT/a = 9.2\times4.1/8 = 4.7\) pN. Under a load \(F\) the backward rates increase (or forward rates decrease) so that the ratio becomes \(e^{9.2 - Fa/k_BT}\), and \(v \to 0\) at \(F_s\).


(Efficiency of kinesin) Kinesin steps \(8\) nm per ATP and stalls at \(6\) pN under conditions where \(\Delta\mu = 25\,k_BT\). Compute the maximum mechanical work per step, the thermodynamic efficiency at stall, and the entropy produced per step at half the stall force.


Solution. Work at stall: \(6\,\text{pN}\times8\,\text{nm} = 48\,\text{pN·nm} = 11.7\,k_BT\). Efficiency \(\eta = 11.7/25 = 47\%\). At \(F = 3\) pN, the work per step is \(24\) pN·nm \(= 5.9\,k_BT\), and the entropy produced per step is \(\Delta S/k_B \geq 25 - 5.9 = 19\,k_BT\): most of the free energy is dissipated as heat when the motor moves at a finite speed.

title: 16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits
text:
16.1 Regulator dynamics
Genes do not act alone: transcription factors produced by some genes regulate the expression of others, forming circuits with recognisable functions. This chapter builds the standard models of transcriptional regulation from binding equilibria (Hill functions), and analyses the basic network motifs: negative autoregulation, which gives homeostasis, faster responses and noise reduction; delayed negative feedback, which gives oscillations; and positive feedback and mutual repression, which give bistable switches and cellular memory. It ends with a combined transport–metabolism circuit (Homework 6) and the generalisation to whole regulatory networks.
crumbs: Part III: Physics of the cell
16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits

title: 16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits
text:
16.1.1 Binding of a regulator
A transcription factor \(R\) binds an operator site \(O\) near a promoter: \(R + O \underset{k_-}{\overset{k_+}{\rightleftharpoons}} RO\). At equilibrium \[\frac{[R][O]}{[RO]} = \frac{k_-}{k_+} = K,\] the dissociation constant (the concentration of \(R\) at which the site is occupied half the time). Since the total number of sites is fixed, \([O] + [RO] = [O_T]\), the occupied fraction is \[f_B([R]) = \frac{[RO]}{[O_T]} = \frac{[R]}{K + [R]}, \qquad f_U = 1 - f_B = \frac{K}{K + [R]}.\]
Often \(h\) regulator molecules bind cooperatively (e.g. as a multimer or at several adjacent sites). For \(hR + O \rightleftharpoons R_hO\) the occupied fraction becomes the Hill function \[f_B = \frac{(R/K)^h}{1 + (R/K)^h}, \qquad f_U = \frac{1}{1 + (R/K)^h},\] with Hill coefficient \(h\) (typically \(1\)–\(4\)). The larger \(h\), the more switch-like the response: for \(h \to \infty\) it becomes a step at \(R = K\).


16.1.2 Activators and repressors
If \(R\) is an activator, the gene is transcribed when the operator is occupied, and its production rate is \(\gamma f_B\). If \(R\) is a repressor, transcription happens when the operator is free, at rate \(\gamma f_U\). Including a basal “leaky” production \(l\) and removal (degradation and dilution) with lifetime \(\tau\), a protein \(X\) regulated by \(R\) obeys \[\frac{dX}{dt} = l + \frac{\gamma}{1 + (R/K)^h} - \frac X\tau \quad\text{(repression)}, \qquad \frac{dX}{dt} = l + \gamma\frac{(R/K)^h}{1 + (R/K)^h} - \frac X\tau \quad\text{(activation)}.\] This is a deterministic, mean-field description. Chapter 14 showed how noise is added.
crumbs: Part III: Physics of the cell
16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits

title: 16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits
text:
16.2 Negative autoregulation

16.2.1 Homeostasis
The most common motif in E. coli (about \(40\%\) of transcription factors) is negative autoregulation (NAR): a repressor represses its own gene, \[\frac{dR}{dt} = l + \frac{\gamma}{1 + (R/K)^h} - \frac R\tau .\] For \(h = 1\) the steady state solves a quadratic, \[R^* = \frac12\Bigl[l\tau - K + \sqrt{K^2 + \tau(l^2\tau + 2Kl + 4K\gamma)}\Bigr],\] and for \(l = 0\), \(R^* \simeq \sqrt{K\gamma\tau}\) when \(\gamma\tau \gg K\). Without regulation \(R^* = (l + \gamma)\tau\), proportional to the production rate \(\gamma\), which depends on the environment (growth conditions, polymerase availability). With NAR it grows only as \(\sqrt\gamma\) for \(h = 1\), and more slowly for larger \(h\): as \(h \to \infty\), \(R^* \to K\) whatever \(\gamma\). The protein level becomes robust to changes in the environment.

With \(l = 0.1\), \(K = \tau = 1\), increasing \(\gamma\) from \(1\) to \(100\) changes the unregulated level from \(1.1\) to \(100\), the \(h = 1\) level from \(0.69\) to \(9.6\), and the \(h = 3\) level only from \(0.78\) to \(3.2\).



16.2.2 Faster responses
NAR also speeds up the response. A gene switched on at \(t = 0\) without regulation reaches half its final level in \(t_{1/2} = \tau\ln2\), independently of the production rate. With NAR the production rate is initially at its maximum (no repressor yet) and is then throttled as \(R\) approaches \(K\), so the steady state is reached much faster. With \(l = 0.5\), \(\gamma = 5\), \(K = \tau = 1\), the time to reach half of \(R^*\) is \(0.34\), \(0.22\), \(0.14\), \(0.12\) for \(h = 1, 2, 5, 8\), against \(0.69\) without regulation. NAR also reduces noise, because fluctuations above the set point lower production and fluctuations below it raise it.


16.2.3 Stress response
Negative feedback through a metabolite gives adaptive stress responses. Let a repressor \(R\) (constant total \(R^*\)) be inactivated by a signal molecule \(S\), \(R_{\text{free}} = R^*/(1 + S)\), and repress an enzyme \(E\) that removes \(S\): \[\frac{dE}{dt} = \frac{1}{1 + R_{\text{free}}^2} - \frac{E}{\tau_E}, \qquad \frac{dS}{dt} = \gamma_r - \alpha ES .\] A sudden increase of the stress input \(\gamma_r\) raises \(S\), frees the gene from repression, and produces the enzyme that brings \(S\) back down. The response is a transient peak followed by adaptation.


16.2.4 Delayed negative feedback: oscillations
Transcription, translation, maturation and transport take time. If the repression acts with a delay \(t_d\), \[\frac{dR}{dt} = l + \frac{\gamma}{1 + \bigl(R(t - t_d)/K\bigr)^h} - \frac R\tau,\] the system overshoots: by the time the repressor acts, too much has been made, then too little. For a sufficiently long delay and steep repression the fixed point loses stability through a Hopf bifurcation and sustained oscillations appear. With \(l = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 10\), \(K = \tau = 1\), \(h = 4\): for \(t_d \leq 0.5\) the level settles at \(1.56\); for \(t_d = 1\) it oscillates between \(0.9\) and \(3.5\); for \(t_d = 2\) between \(0.5\) and \(7.5\). Delayed negative feedback underlies circadian clocks, the p53–Mdm2 oscillations after DNA damage, and the synthetic repressilator (three genes repressing each other in a ring; Elowitz and Leibler, 2000).

title: 16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits
text:
16.3 Positive feedback and bistability

16.3.1 The toggle switch
Two repressors \(R\) and \(L\) that repress each other form a double-negative, i.e. effectively positive, feedback loop: \[\frac{dR}{dt} = l_R + \frac{\gamma}{1 + L^{h_L}} - \frac{R}{\tau_R}, \qquad \frac{dL}{dt} = l_L + \frac{\gamma}{1 + R^{h_R}} - \frac{L}{\tau_L},\] in units where \(K = 1\). For \(h = 1\) there is a single symmetric steady state. For \(h > 1\) and strong enough repression there are three: two stable states, one with \(R\) high and \(L\) low and one with the opposite, separated by an unstable symmetric state. For example, with \(l = 0\), \(\gamma = 4\), \(\tau = 1\), \(h = 2\) the steady states are \((3.73, 0.27)\), \((0.27, 3.73)\) and \((1.38, 1.38)\).
The circuit is a genetic switch: a transient signal that pushes the system across the separatrix flips it to the other state, which then persists after the signal is gone. The cell has a memory of past signals, inherited by its daughters, an epigenetic state not encoded in the DNA sequence. The phage λ lysis–lysogeny decision is the classic natural example (the cI and Cro repressors), and Gardner, Cantor and Collins (2000) built a synthetic toggle switch in E. coli. Cooperativity (\(h > 1\)) is essential: without it the nullclines cross only once.


16.3.2 Self-activation
A gene that activates itself, \(\dot X = l + \gamma\frac{X^h}{1 + X^h} - X/\tau\), is bistable for \(h > 1\) in a range of parameters: an “off” state at \(X \simeq l\tau\) and an “on” state near \((l + \gamma)\tau\). Positive feedback converts graded inputs into all-or-none, irreversible decisions (differentiation, sporulation, competence), and noise can trigger spontaneous switching between the states (Chapter 14).
crumbs: Part III: Physics of the cell
16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits

title: 16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits
text:
16.4 Combining loops: transport and metabolism
Real circuits combine both kinds of feedback. Consider a cell taking up a nutrient \(S\) (e.g. lactose) through a transport protein \(T\) and consuming it with an enzyme \(E\), both repressed by a regulator \(R\) that is inactivated by \(S\), \(R_{\text{free}} = R^*/(1 + S)\): \[\frac{dS}{dt} = \sigma T - \gamma ES - S, \qquad \frac{dT}{dt} = l + \frac{1}{1 + (R_{\text{free}}/K_T)^h} - T, \qquad \frac{dE}{dt} = l + \frac{1}{1 + (R_{\text{free}}/K_E)^h} - E .\] The transport loop is positive: more \(S\) frees more repressor, which makes more transporter, which imports more \(S\). The metabolic loop is negative: more \(S\) makes more enzyme, which consumes \(S\). The positive loop makes the response to the external supply \(\sigma\) steep and possibly bistable (the “all-or-none” induction of the lac operon observed by Novick and Weiner, 1957). The negative loop keeps the internal concentration of \(S\) in check. With \(R^* = 10\), \(K_T = K_E = 1\), \(h = 2\), \(l = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 1\): for \(\sigma = 1\) and \(10\) the circuit stays almost uninduced (\(T = E \simeq 0.11\)–\(0.15\)), while for \(\sigma = 100\) it is fully induced (\(T = E \simeq 1.07\), \(S \simeq 52\)).
crumbs: Part III: Physics of the cell
16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits

title: 16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits
text:
16.5 From motifs to networks
For many genes the same approach gives a generalised dynamics \[\frac{dx_i}{dt} = -x_i + \sum_{j=1}^NA_{ij}\frac{x_j^h}{1 + x_j^h},\] where \(A_{ij}\) encodes the gene regulatory network (activation \(A_{ij} > 0\), repression \(A_{ij} < 0\)). This is formally a recurrent neural network (Chapter 10) or a generalised Lotka–Volterra system (Chapter 6). Its many stable states can be identified with cell types, an idea going back to Kauffman and formalised as a Hopfield network whose attractors are cell identities (Waddington’s epigenetic landscape). Chapter 17 asks the inverse question: how to infer \(A\) from measured expression patterns.
crumbs: Part III: Physics of the cell
16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits

title: 16  Gene regulation and genetic circuits
text:
16.6 Exercises

(HW 6.1) Feedback loops. Choose one of the feedback loops discussed in class (negative or positive) and simulate it.


Solution. Negative autoregulation (\(l = 0.5\), \(\gamma = 5\), \(K = \tau = 1\)). Integrating from \(R(0) = 0\), the trajectories converge to \(R^* = 2.11\), \(1.74\), \(1.37\), \(1.24\) for \(h = 1, 2, 5, 8\), matching the root of \(l + \gamma/(1 + R^h) = R\) and the closed form for \(h = 1\). As \(h\) grows, \(R^*\) approaches the large-\(h\) limit, where \(R^* \simeq K = 1\) if \(\tau(l + \gamma) > K\). Half-times are \(0.34\), \(0.22\), \(0.14\), \(0.12\), all shorter than the unregulated \(\ln2 = 0.69\): NAR speeds up the response. Homeostasis: as \(\gamma\) varies from \(1\) to \(100\) (with \(l = 0.1\)), \(R^*\) grows tenfold for \(h = 1\) and fourfold for \(h = 3\), against a hundredfold without regulation.
Positive feedback (toggle switch, \(\gamma = 4\), \(h = 2\)). Trajectories from different initial conditions end in one of two stable states, \((3.73, 0.27)\) or \((0.27, 3.73)\), according to which side of the diagonal they start. A transient pulse of inducer that lowers one repressor flips the switch permanently.


(HW 6.2) Combining loops. Combine two feedback loops (for instance the transport–metabolism network shown in class), simulate it, and describe what happens.


Solution. With the model of the text (\(R^* = 10\), \(K_T = K_E = 1\), \(h = 2\), \(l = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 1\)), integrating to steady state for increasing supply: \(\sigma = 1\), \((S, T, E) = (0.10, 0.11, 0.11)\); \(\sigma = 10\), \((1.31, 0.15, 0.15)\); \(\sigma = 100\), \((51.6, 1.07, 1.07)\). At low supply the repressor is mostly free and the genes are off. When enough nutrient enters, it titrates the repressor, transporter and enzyme are induced, and uptake jumps (positive loop), while the enzyme limits the accumulation of \(S\) (negative loop). The induction is switch-like in \(\sigma\). Making the transporter more sensitive than the enzyme (\(K_T < K_E\)) shifts the induction to lower supplies and can produce bistability and hysteresis: cells grown with the nutrient remain induced at supplies that cannot induce naive cells, a memory of past exposure.


(Hill functions) Show that the steepness of the Hill function at \(R = K\) is \(\frac{d f_B}{d\ln R} = h/4\), and compute the fold change in \(R\) needed to go from \(10\%\) to \(90\%\) occupancy.


Solution. \(f_B = \frac{x^h}{1 + x^h}\) with \(x = R/K\), so \(\frac{df_B}{d\ln R} = h f_B(1 - f_B) = h/4\) at \(x = 1\). \(f_B = 0.1\) at \(x^h = 1/9\) and \(0.9\) at \(x^h = 9\), so \(x_{90}/x_{10} = 81^{1/h}\): \(81\)-fold for \(h = 1\), \(9\)-fold for \(h = 2\), \(3\)-fold for \(h = 4\). Cooperativity turns a gradual response into a switch.


(Bistability of self-activation) For \(\dot X = \frac{X^2}{1 + X^2} - \frac X\tau\) (no leak, \(\gamma = K = 1\)), find the steady states and the range of \(\tau\) for bistability.


Solution. \(X = 0\) is always a steady state. Non-zero ones satisfy \(\frac{X}{1 + X^2} = \frac1\tau\), i.e. \(X^2 - \tau X + 1 = 0\), so \(X_\pm = \frac{\tau \pm\sqrt{\tau^2 - 4}}{2}\), real for \(\tau > 2\). For \(\tau > 2\) there are three states: \(0\) (stable), \(X_-\) (unstable) and \(X_+\) (stable). The cell is bistable once the protein lives long enough to sustain its own production. With \(h = 1\) instead, \(\frac{X}{1 + X} = \frac X\tau\) has only \(X = \tau - 1\) besides \(0\), so there is no bistability.

title: 17  Inferring gene interaction networks by maximum entropy
text:
17.1 Gene expression data
Chapter 16 started from known regulatory interactions and predicted the dynamics. In practice the problem is reversed: we measure the expression of thousands of genes in many samples or single cells, and want to infer who regulates whom. This chapter treats network inference as a statistical-physics inverse problem. The maximum-entropy principle gives the least biased model that reproduces the measured means and correlations. For Gaussian data the inferred interaction matrix is the inverse of the covariance matrix, which separates direct interactions from indirect correlations. For binarised single-cell data, a kinetic (asymmetric) Ising model learned from time-ordered cells yields directed, signed networks able to predict the effect of perturbations.
A typical dataset is a matrix of counts \(n_{it}\): the number of mRNA reads of gene \(i = 1, \dots, N\) in sample (or cell) \(t = 1, \dots, T\). Before analysis, raw counts are normalised for sequencing depth (\(\sum_in_{it}\)) and gene length \(L_i\), and log-transformed: \[x_{it} = \log\frac{n_{it}}{L_i\,\sum_jn_{jt}} \quad\text{(up to constants)}.\] Bulk RNA-seq averages millions of cells per sample. Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) measures individual cells, revealing heterogeneity and transitions between states, but each cell is measured only once (it is destroyed). Dynamics must be reconstructed from snapshots, e.g. by ordering cells along a pseudotime of differentiation.
From the data we can estimate the means \(\langle x_i\rangle\) and the pairwise correlations \(\langle x_ix_j\rangle\). Ideally we would like the full joint distribution \(p(x_1, \dots, x_N)\), but with \(N \sim 10^4\) genes and \(T \ll\) the number of possible states, it cannot be estimated directly. A principled proxy is needed.

title: 17  Inferring gene interaction networks by maximum entropy
text:
17.2 The maximum-entropy principle
Among all distributions consistent with what we know, choose the one that assumes nothing else: the one maximising the entropy \(S[\rho] = -\sum_{\mathbf x}\rho(\mathbf x)\ln\rho(\mathbf x)\) (Jaynes, 1957). Imposing normalisation, the means and the second moments, with Lagrange multipliers \(\nu\), \(\psi_i\) and \(\lambda_{ij}\), \[\mathcal S = S[\rho] - \nu\Bigl(\sum\rho - 1\Bigr) - \sum_i\psi_i\Bigl(\sum\rho\,x_i - \langle x_i\rangle\Bigr) - \sum_{i\leq j}\lambda_{ij}\Bigl(\sum\rho\,x_ix_j - \langle x_ix_j\rangle\Bigr).\] Setting \(\delta\mathcal S/\delta\rho = 0\): \[\rho(\mathbf x) = \frac1Z\exp\Bigl(-\boldsymbol\psi\cdot\mathbf x - \frac12\mathbf x^\top M\mathbf x\Bigr), \qquad M_{ij} = \lambda_{ij} + \lambda_{ji}.\]

17.2.1 Continuous expression levels
For continuous \(x\) the maximum-entropy distribution is a multivariate Gaussian. Completing the square, \(\mathbf y = \mathbf x + M^{-1}\boldsymbol\psi\), it is centred at \(\langle\mathbf x\rangle = -M^{-1}\boldsymbol\psi\) with covariance \[C_{ij} = \langle x_ix_j\rangle - \langle x_i\rangle\langle x_j\rangle = (M^{-1})_{ij} .\] So the interaction matrix is the inverse of the covariance matrix (the precision matrix): \[M = C^{-1} .\] The model has \(N + N(N + 1)/2\) parameters, exactly the number of constraints, and the “Hamiltonian” \(H = \frac12\mathbf x^\top M\mathbf x + \boldsymbol\psi\cdot\mathbf x\) reads \(M_{ij}\) as the effective interaction between genes \(i\) and \(j\).






Correlation is not interaction. If gene \(A\) regulates \(B\) and \(B\) regulates \(C\), then \(A\) and \(C\) are correlated although they do not interact directly. Biologists often build “co-expression networks” by thresholding correlations, which mixes direct and indirect effects. The inverse covariance removes the indirect contributions: \(M_{ij}\) is proportional to the partial correlation of \(i\) and \(j\) given all other genes, and is zero when \(i\) and \(j\) are conditionally independent.





17.2.2 The undersampled regime
With \(T < N\) samples the empirical covariance matrix has rank at most \(T\) and cannot be inverted. Lezon et al. (2006) used the spectral decomposition \[C = \sum_{k=1}^N\omega_k\,\mathbf v^{(k)}\mathbf v^{(k)\top},\] keeping only the \(T - 1\) non-zero eigenvalues and defining the pseudo-inverse \(M = \sum_{k:\omega_k > 0}\omega_k^{-1}\mathbf v^{(k)}\mathbf v^{(k)\top}\). Regularised alternatives (ridge, the graphical lasso with an \(\ell_1\) penalty that favours sparse \(M\)) are used in practice.


17.2.3 Are pairwise interactions enough?
The maximum-entropy model can be extended with three-body terms, \(H \supset \sum T_{ijk}x_ix_jx_k\). Applied to time series of yeast gene expression during the metabolic cycle, the distribution of inferred pairwise couplings is broad, while that of triplet couplings is narrowly centred on zero (Lezon et al., 2006): pairwise interactions dominate. Significance is assessed with a null model: shuffling the data table independently for each gene destroys correlations while preserving single-gene statistics, and couplings within the null distribution are discarded. The inferred networks show a hub-dominated structure, with modules matching functional categories (translation, transcription, cell division, mitochondria, ribosome biogenesis).

text:
17.3 Binary expression and the Ising model
For many purposes it is enough to know whether a gene is “on” or “off”. Binarising each gene’s expression relative to a threshold (e.g. half its maximum), \[s_i(t) = \begin{cases}+1 & x_i(t) \geq \frac12\max_tx_i\\ -1 & \text{otherwise},\end{cases}\] the maximum-entropy distribution with fixed means and pairwise correlations is the Ising model of Chapter 12, \[P(\mathbf s) = \frac1Z\exp\Bigl(\sum_ih_is_i + \sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j\Bigr),\] with symmetric couplings. Symmetric couplings cannot represent the direction of regulation (\(A\) activates \(B\) but not vice versa) and are learned from equal-time statistics only.

title: 17  Inferring gene interaction networks by maximum entropy
text:
17.5 Exercises

(Maximum entropy with fixed mean and variance) Show that the maximum-entropy density on \(\mathbb R\) with fixed mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) is the Gaussian, and that with only the mean fixed on \([0, \infty)\) it is the exponential.


Solution. Stationarity of \(-\int\rho\ln\rho - \nu(\int\rho - 1) - \psi(\int x\rho - \mu) - \lambda(\int x^2\rho - \sigma^2 - \mu^2)\) gives \(-\ln\rho - 1 - \nu - \psi x - \lambda x^2 = 0\), so \(\rho \propto e^{-\psi x - \lambda x^2}\), a Gaussian whose parameters are fixed by the constraints (\(\lambda = 1/2\sigma^2\), \(\psi = -\mu/\sigma^2\)). With only the mean on \([0, \infty)\), \(\rho \propto e^{-\psi x}\): the exponential with \(\psi = 1/\mu\). Maximum entropy reproduces the familiar distributions as the least informative ones given the constraints, and the Lagrange multipliers play the role of couplings.


(Correlation versus interaction) Three genes form a chain \(A - B - C\) with Gaussian interaction matrix \(M = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -0.4 & 0\\ -0.4 & 1 & -0.4\\ 0 & -0.4 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). Compute the correlation matrix. Would thresholding correlations at \(0.15\) recover the true network?


Solution. \(C = M^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1.235 & 0.588 & 0.235\\ 0.588 & 1.471 & 0.588\\ 0.235 & 0.588 & 1.235\end{pmatrix}\), giving correlation coefficients \(\rho_{AB} = \rho_{BC} = 0.44\) and \(\rho_{AC} = 0.19\). Thresholding at \(0.15\) would add a spurious \(A\)–\(C\) link. The partial correlations \(-M_{ij}/\sqrt{M_{ii}M_{jj}}\) are \(0.4\) for \(A\)–\(B\) and \(B\)–\(C\) and exactly \(0\) for \(A\)–\(C\): inverting the covariance removes the indirect correlation mediated by \(B\).


(Pseudo-inverse) With \(N = 1000\) genes and \(T = 50\) samples, how many eigenvalues of the empirical covariance matrix are non-zero? What does the pseudo-inverse do, and what is its main limitation?


Solution. After subtracting the sample mean, the centred data matrix has rank at most \(T - 1 = 49\), so at most \(49\) eigenvalues are non-zero and \(951\) vanish. The pseudo-inverse inverts \(C\) on the \(49\)-dimensional subspace spanned by the data and sets \(M\) to zero on its complement. Interactions are thus inferred only along the directions the data explore, and the smallest non-zero eigenvalues, dominated by sampling noise, are amplified by \(1/\omega_k\). Regularisation (truncating small eigenvalues, ridge or lasso penalties) controls this noise at the cost of bias.


(Kinetic Ising learning) For a single gene \(i\) driven by a single gene \(j\), \(\theta_i = h + Js_j\), show that the maximum-likelihood conditions are \(\langle s_i^{\text{next}}\rangle = \langle\tanh\theta_i\rangle\) and \(\langle s_i^{\text{next}}s_j\rangle = \langle\tanh\theta_i\,s_j\rangle\). If \(s_j = \pm1\) with equal probability and \(s_i^{\text{next}} = s_j\) in \(90\%\) of the updates, what are \(h\) and \(J\)?


Solution. \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial h = \sum[s_i^{\text{next}} - \tanh\theta_i]\) and \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial J = \sum[s_i^{\text{next}} - \tanh\theta_i]s_j\); setting both to zero gives the conditions. By symmetry \(h = 0\). Then \(\tanh\theta_i\,s_j = \tanh(J)\) for both values of \(s_j\), and \(\langle s_i^{\text{next}}s_j\rangle = 0.9 - 0.1 = 0.8\). So \(\tanh J = 0.8\) and \(J = \operatorname{artanh}0.8 = 1.10\). The coupling from \(j\) to \(i\) is positive (activation). The reverse coupling \(J_{ji}\) is learned separately from the updates of \(j\), and may be zero.

title: 18  Proteins as physical objects: polymers, folding and the tube model
text:
18.1 Homopolymers: scaling laws
Proteins are the working molecules of the cell: enzymes, motors, channels, transcription factors. Each is a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific three-dimensional shape that determines its function. Can polymer physics explain why protein structures are what they are? This chapter recalls the scaling theory of homopolymers (ideal chains, self-avoiding chains, compact globules), lists the experimental facts that make proteins special, and presents the tube model of Banavar and Maritan. Treating the chain as a tube of finite thickness, rather than a string of beads, generates the menu of secondary structures (helices and sheets) from geometry and symmetry alone. The chapter ends with an outlook on topics treated in the course projects.
A polymer is a chain of \(L\) similar monomers at positions \(\mathbf r_1, \dots, \mathbf r_L\). Its size is measured by the end-to-end distance \(R_L = |\mathbf r_L - \mathbf r_1|\) or the radius of gyration \(R_G^2 = \frac1L\sum_i(\mathbf r_i - \mathbf R_c)^2\). Both scale with length as \[R \sim L^\nu ,\] with a universal exponent \(\nu\) that depends only on the dimension and on the phase of the polymer, not on chemical details, beyond the persistence length.

title: 18  Proteins as physical objects: polymers, folding and the tube model
text:
18.1.1 Ideal chains
If the chain can cross itself (no excluded volume), it is a random walk of \(L/\ell_p\) independent segments of length \(\sim\ell_p\) (the persistence length). By the central limit theorem the end-to-end vector is Gaussian, \[P_{\text{ideal}}(\mathbf R \mid L) = \Bigl(\frac{3}{2\pi L\ell_p}\Bigr)^{3/2}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{3R^2}{2L\ell_p}\Bigr), \qquad \langle R^2\rangle = L\ell_p, \qquad \nu = \frac12 .\] The Gaussian form has an entropic interpretation: the free energy \(F(R) = -k_BT\ln P = \frac{3k_BTR^2}{2L\ell_p}\) is that of an entropic spring. Stretching a chain reduces the number of its conformations, which is why rubber is elastic.


18.1.2 Self-avoiding chains: Flory’s argument
Real chains cannot overlap. Excluded volume swells them, with \(\nu > 1/2\). Flory’s estimate balances the elastic entropy against the repulsion between monomers in a volume \(R^d\): \[\frac{F(R)}{k_BT} \simeq \frac{R^2}{L\ell_p} + v\frac{L^2}{R^d} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R \sim L^{\nu_F}, \qquad \nu_F = \frac{3}{d + 2}.\] This gives \(\nu = 3/5\) in \(d = 3\) (the exact value is \(0.588\)), \(3/4\) in \(d = 2\) (exact), and \(1/2\) at the upper critical dimension \(d = 4\). The end-to-end distribution of a self-avoiding chain is non-Gaussian, with the scaling form \(P_{\text{real}}(\mathbf R \mid L) \propto x^{\theta}e^{-x^{\delta}}\), \(x = R/L^\nu\), \(\delta = 1/(1 - \nu)\).


18.1.3 Good and poor solvents
Monomers also attract each other with an energy that competes with solvent affinity. In a good solvent (high temperature) the chain is swollen (\(\nu = 0.588\)). In a poor solvent (low temperature) attraction wins and the chain collapses into a compact globule that fills space, so \(R \sim L^{1/3}\). At the \(\Theta\)-point between them, the second virial coefficient vanishes and the chain is nearly ideal (\(\nu = 1/2\)). Flory’s theorem states that in a dense, compact polymer a sub-chain of length \(\ell\) behaves as ideal, \(R_G(\ell) \sim \ell^{1/2}\), because excluded volume is screened by the other chains.
The compact phase of standard models (beads on a string with pair potentials, or the Edwards continuum model \(H = \int ds\,[\dot{\mathbf r}^2 + \kappa\ddot{\mathbf r}^2] + v\iint ds\,ds'\,\delta(\mathbf r(s) - \mathbf r(s'))\)) is either a crystal of Hamiltonian walks or a disordered liquid-like globule. Its number of conformations grows exponentially, \(\mathcal N(L) \sim L^{\gamma - 1}\mu^L\), and none of them is special. This is very far from proteins.

title: 18  Proteins as physical objects: polymers, folding and the tube model
text:
18.2 What makes proteins special
A protein is a heteropolymer of \(20\) amino acids, with a backbone (\(\text{N}\)–\(\text{C}_\alpha\)–\(\text{C}'\)) and side chains of different sizes and chemistry (hydrophobic, polar, charged). Experiments show:

Proteins fold rapidly (microseconds to seconds) and reproducibly into a native state.
The native geometry determines function.
The number of distinct folds is small, a few thousand, much less than the number of sequences.
Many different sequences fold into the same structure: folds are robust to mutations.
Structures are built from a few modular secondary motifs: \(\alpha\)-helices and almost-planar \(\beta\)-sheets, as predicted by Pauling and Corey (1951) from hydrogen-bond geometry.
Proteins with the same fold have similar folding rates and transition states.
Native structures are flexible and interact with ligands and with each other in versatile ways. Misfolded proteins can aggregate into amyloid fibrils (sheet-rich structures common to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases) that any sequence can form.

Levinthal’s paradox (1969): if each residue of a \(100\)-residue protein had \(3\) conformations, a random search among \(3^{100} \simeq 5\times10^{47}\) states at \(10^{13}\) per second would take \(\sim 10^{27}\) years. Folding must follow a biased funnel-shaped energy landscape, not a random search. These facts suggest that the menu of folds is determined by general physical principles shared by all sequences, with the sequence choosing among a few pre-sculpted possibilities.

18  Proteins as physical objects: polymers, folding and the tube model

title: 18  Proteins as physical objects: polymers, folding and the tube model
text:
18.3 The tube model

18.3.1 Thickness as a missing ingredient
A string of beads with pair potentials has a symmetry that a real chain lacks. Each backbone unit is not a sphere but closer to a coin, a flat object with a preferred orientation, because of the planar peptide bond and the direction of the side chain. In the continuum limit, a chain of spheres becomes a line of zero thickness, while a chain of coins becomes a tube of finite thickness. A pair potential between points of a curve is singular: nearby points along the chain are always close, so the potential needs a cut-off, i.e. a fundamental length the model lacks.
The thickness of a curve is captured by three-body interactions (Gonzalez and Maddocks, 1999). For any three points \(s, s', s''\) of the curve, let \(R(s, s', s'')\) be the radius of the circle through them. As the points merge it tends to the local radius of curvature. The thickness of the curve is \[\Delta = \min_{s,s',s''}R(s, s', s''),\] the radius of the largest tube that can be inflated around the curve without self-intersection. A tube of thickness \(\Delta\) is described by forbidding conformations with any \(R(s, s', s'') < \Delta\): a non-singular, three-body constraint that respects the symmetry of the chain.


18.3.2 Optimal packing: the magic helix
What shapes does a compact tube adopt? Maximise compactness at fixed thickness, the polymer analogue of Kepler’s sphere packing. The answer is a helix with a specific geometry: the densest packed single helix has pitch-to-radius ratio \(p/r \simeq 2.512\), within \(5\%\) of real \(\alpha\)-helices (Maritan, Micheletti, Trovato, Banavar, Nature 2000). The densest double helix has \(p/r = 2\pi\), within \(4\%\) of B-DNA (\(6.03\)). Other optimal configurations are planar zig-zag sheets, which pack side by side like \(\beta\)-sheets. Secondary structures emerge from geometry, not from the chemical details of hydrogen bonds, which then fit into them.


18.3.3 The marginally compact phase
Add a solvophobic attraction proportional to the buried surface (energy \(\simeq -\) area of the tube not exposed to solvent), with a range comparable to the thickness. As temperature and the ratio of interaction range to thickness vary, the tube has a swollen phase, a compact phase, and between them a marginally compact phase. There the tube is just compact enough to bury its surface but still constrained by its thickness. In this phase:

the number of low-energy conformations is small: the degeneracy that plagues standard polymers is lifted;
the ground states are rich in helices and sheets, assembled into a few thousand distinct topologies resembling real folds;
the free-energy landscape is pre-sculpted by geometry and symmetry, and the sequence only has to choose one of a few competing minima. This explains robustness to mutations, fast folding, and the fact that unrelated sequences share folds.

Proteins appear to sit near a phase transition, in the marginally compact phase. The same structures make them prone to aggregation (amyloids, a generic sheet-rich state) and give intrinsically disordered proteins a natural place: sequences that do not select any minimum.

title: 18  Proteins as physical objects: polymers, folding and the tube model
text:
18.4 Outlook: from cells to communities
The course projects connect the three modules:

Clonal stem-cell dynamics. Stem cells divide symmetrically or asymmetrically and differentiate stochastically. Master equations for clone sizes, like those of Chapters 2–3, predict clone-size distributions to compare with lineage-tracing data (Greulich, 2019).
The Waddington landscape. Cell types as attractors of gene regulatory networks, modelled as Hopfield networks whose stored patterns are expression profiles (Chapters 11 and 16). Differentiation is a descent in a landscape, and reprogramming a forced jump between basins.
Microbiomes. Human gut microbial communities show macroecological patterns (abundance distributions, Taylor’s law, abundance fluctuations) captured by stochastic logistic models with environmental noise (Chapter 2) and by disordered Lotka–Volterra models (Chapter 6). Changes of their parameters can describe the transition to dysbiosis.
Eco-evolutionary dynamics. Strains within a species interact and evolve on ecological time scales; consumer–resource models with adaptive metabolism (Chapter 7) connect metabolic networks to community assembly.

A guest lecture (A. Forli) illustrated the neuroscience frontier. In freely flying Egyptian fruit bats, hippocampal neurons encode the bat’s own position and also social information about group members. Ensembles of place cells “replay” flight trajectories in time-compressed form during rest. Event-based cameras enable microsecond imaging of neural activity. Comparative studies across species test whether mechanisms such as theta sequences, believed to be universal, really are.

title: 18  Proteins as physical objects: polymers, folding and the tube model
text:
18.5 Exercises

(Ideal chain) Show that for an ideal chain of \(n = L/\ell_p\) independent segments of length \(\ell_p\) with isotropic directions, \(\langle R^2\rangle = n\ell_p^2\), and derive the entropic force needed to hold the ends at distance \(R\).


Solution. \(\mathbf R = \sum_k\mathbf b_k\) with \(|\mathbf b_k| = \ell_p\) and \(\langle\mathbf b_k\cdot\mathbf b_l\rangle = \ell_p^2\delta_{kl}\), so \(\langle R^2\rangle = n\ell_p^2 = L\ell_p\). By the central limit theorem \(P(\mathbf R) \propto e^{-3R^2/(2n\ell_p^2)}\), and \(F = -k_BT\ln P = \frac{3k_BT}{2n\ell_p^2}R^2 + \text{const}\). The force is \(f = \partial F/\partial R = \frac{3k_BT}{n\ell_p^2}R\): a Hookean spring with stiffness proportional to temperature. Because it is entropic, the chain gets stiffer when heated.


(Flory exponent) Minimise \(F/k_BT = R^2/(L\ell_p) + vL^2/R^d\) with respect to \(R\) and derive \(\nu_F\). Evaluate it in \(d = 1, 2, 3, 4\) and compare with exact values.


Solution. \(\partial_RF = 2R/(L\ell_p) - dvL^2/R^{d+1} = 0\) gives \(R^{d+2} \propto L^3\), so \(\nu_F = 3/(d + 2)\): \(1\) in \(d = 1\) (exact, a stretched chain), \(3/4\) in \(d = 2\) (exact), \(3/5\) in \(d = 3\) (exact \(0.588\)), \(1/2\) in \(d = 4\) (exact, mean field from here on). Flory’s argument works so well because errors in the two terms nearly cancel.


(Levinthal’s paradox) Estimate the time for an exhaustive search of the conformations of a \(100\)-residue protein with \(3\) states per residue, sampling \(10^{13}\) conformations per second. How does a funnel resolve the paradox?


Solution. \(3^{100} = 5.2\times10^{47}\) conformations, so the search time is \(5.2\times10^{34}\) s \(\approx 1.6\times10^{27}\) years, against a real folding time of milliseconds. In a funnel each residue’s conformation is stabilised as soon as it is locally correct: errors are not frozen but corrected, so the search is biased toward the native state. If each residue finds its local state independently in time \(\tau\), folding takes \(\sim\tau\ln L\) instead of \(\sim\tau\,3^L\). A modest energetic bias per residue (\(\sim k_BT\)) suffices.


(Compact-state entropy) A compact polymer of \(L\) monomers has \(\mathcal N \sim\mu^L\) conformations with \(\mu \approx 1.4\) (cubic lattice). Compare the number of compact conformations of a \(100\)-residue chain with the number of distinct protein folds. What does this say about standard polymer models?


Solution. \(1.4^{100} \simeq 4\times10^{14}\) compact conformations, all of comparable energy in a homopolymer model, against about \(10^3\) observed folds. A standard compact homopolymer has an enormous ground-state degeneracy and no reason to prefer helices or sheets. The tube model reduces the number of competing low-energy structures to a few, rich in secondary motifs, matching the observed “menu” of folds.
